speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE LATE VITAL MALLETTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I deeply
regret to have to inform the house that I received only about an hour ago word of the sudden passing of one of our hon. members, Mr. Vital Mallette, the representative in this house of the Constituency of Jacques-Cartier. Word came to me in a telegram from an hon. member who informed me that at the noon hour to-day, or a little before noon, Mr. Mallette had been stricken with heart failure and had passed away while walking on the street in Montreal. I know that this word will come as a great shock to all hon. members. While Mr. Mallette had been a member of the commons only since the last general election, he was possessed of such a pleasant personality, he took such an active part in the general affairs of parliament, was so kind and

The late Vital Mallette
generous and friendly, and was so much liked, that in his passing I am sure all hon. members will experience a sense of real personal loss.
Mr. Mallette was in his fifty-first year. He was born at Pointe Claire. While he played an important part in provincial and national affairs his life was identified, in an intimate way, almost exclusively, with that municipality and the more varied activities and interests of Montreal. He served as an alderman of Pointe Claire for a number of years and for two or three years was mayor of the municipality. At the time of his death he was acting as secretary-treasurer of the municipality. The meritorious nature of his services in municipal affairs was recognized by one foreign government and was widely appreciated throughout the province in which he lived. Mr. Mallette was deeply solicitous of the welfare of his constituents and was most faithful in the discharge of his duties in this house.
It is mutely eloquent of Mr. Mallette's wide interest in affairs that on the order paper of to-day there appears a question in his name with respect to Canada's trade with Spain. Hon. members will recall that our late friend was much interested in social and international affairs. His life was given largely to an effort to further human betterment. His interest in young people, in particular, was deep and constant. The advancement of their welfare by the creation of national scholarships will be present in the minds of those who heard him advocate that proposal upon the floor of this house.
I might say very much with reference to the loss to our country which the sudden passing of one so gifted and so full of promise means at this time. I shall take occasion to speak of that on some future occasion. I will only say at the moment that those of us who sit on this side of the house have suffered an irreparable loss in the passing of one who was greatly loved by all the members of his party, who was exceptionally loyal to its policies and principles and at all times faithful in his devotion to its leader.
To Mrs. Mallette and her four children who have been so suddenly and so greatly bereaved there will go forth the deepest sympathy of hon. members from all sides of this house.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Leader of the Opposition) :
maintopic: THE LATE VITAL MALLETTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it comes to us always with a shock when anyone is carried away in the prime of life, and to die at fifty-one is certainly to pass away in the very prime; but the shock is all the greater when the deceased is one with whom we have been in contact and whom we know fairly well. I had not the honour of a personal acquaintance with
Mr. Mallette prior to the present session, but I know of his long public service in the city of Montreal and its surroundings, and I do know this, that he was greatly beloved by all members on this side of the house. For example, on my way into the chamber this afternoon at least half a dozen of our members expressed to me their deep affection for Mr. Mallette. They spoke of his kindly disposition, his genial personality, the fine friendly spirit which at all times he manifested to alt of us. So for that reason at least, on behalf of this party I can speak very highly of him. For myself, I had a few contacts with him, and on the occasions on which I heard him in this chamber I admired his ability to express himself. I sincerely join with the Prime Minister in expressing to the family of Mr. Mallette our very deep sympathy, and that sympathy I also wish to convey to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself and his party in the loss of an active and able representative.

maintopic: THE LATE VITAL MALLETTE
speechtext: On behalf of the group with which I am associated I wish to express regret at the sudden passing of one whom we have grown to respect and for whom many of us who come from other parts of Canada have conceived something of an affection. As one of those who come from western Canada, an English-speaking part of the dominion, I should like to say that Mr. Mallette was one of those in the house who have contributed to the well-being of the Dominion of Canada, inasmuch as he interpreted to us some of the thoughts and aspirations of the French-Cana-dian people from which he came. We deeply regret his passing. We should like to associate ourselves with those who have expressed sympathy for the bereaved family, and we also sympathize with the Prime Minister and the party to which Mr. Mallette belonged in the loss they have sustained.

maintopic: THE LATE VITAL MALLETTE
speechtext:
As one of the members from the island of Montreal I desire to express for myself and, I am quite sure, for all my colleagues, our profound sorrow at the sudden and untimely death of Mr. Mallette. I had known him only foy reputation until he entered . the house. That reputation was high and well-merited, as I have come to know during the past three sessions. I do not exaggerate in saying that he was a model member, devoted to the interests of his constituency, a broadminded, tolerant man. His constituency contains a large percentage of English people, and among them he numbered only friends. Ha had the happy faculty, perhaps a somewhat
The late Vital Mallette

rare one, of making friends, and I venture to say that no one could come in contact with Mr. Mallette without conceiving the highest possible regard for him. He never introduced party feeling into his social or his personal relations. Wherever he was known he was not only respected but greatly liked, and his constituency, the province of Quebec, and this House of Commons have suffered no mean loss in the regrettable and lamented death of Mr. Mallette.

maintopic: THE LATE VITAL MALLETTE
speechtext: On behalf of the group with which I am associated and of myself I desire to join in the expressions of sympathy which have been tendered the bereaved family in the death of Mr. Mallette. Mr. Mallette was a member of an opposing party whom I came to know very well indeed. I can go further and say that it was only in his honour and behalf that I have ever worn a ribbon distinctive of the Liberal party. I well remember the occasion on which his constituents tendered him a banquet upon his first being elected to the House of Commons, and Mr. Vital Mallette, out of the kindness of his heart, invited me to participate. From that time many members of our group became closely acquainted with him, and the news of his death to-day has come to us as a distinct shock. We wish to join with the others in offering sympathy both to Mr. Mallette's family and to the :government, who have lost a man of whom they might very well be proud.

speakeroldname: Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Public Works) (Translation):
maintopic: THE LATE VITAL MALLETTE
speechtext: The terrifying news of the death of Mr. Vital Mallette has deeply saddened all the members of the house and more particularly the representatives of the French element of the population. Mr. Mallette, as the Prime Minister (Mr Mackenzie King) has so aptly said, was an exemplary man. Unassuming, most attentive to his various duties, profoundly devoted to his family, he was a remarkable citizen. In the province of Quebec, indeed throughout all Canada, the premature death of this eminently useful and respectable citizen will be greatly regretted. I wish to join the Prime Minister in offering my heartfelt sympathy to Mrs. Mallette and all the members of her family.

maintopic: THE LATE VITAL MALLETTE
speechtext: Not only have I lost my deskmate, but I believe this house will always remember the late Mr. Mallette as one of the most lovable and popular associates. In this hour of sorrow we extend to his wife and family our deepest sympathy.

maintopic: THE LATE VITAL MALLETTE
speechtext: I, too, loved Mr. Mallette and admired his excellent qualities so continuously displayed. I desire that my sympathy with his family be extended through you, sir.

maintopic: THE LATE VITAL MALLETTE
speechtext:
Mr. Mallette was such a dear and valued friend of ours in this part of the house that I simply cannot let this occasion pass without paying a humble tribute to his memory. In this part of the house we were like a family, of which he was a most beloved member. His memory will always be held dear by all of us.
I count it a great privilege to have known him and so to have come under the influence of as fine a Christian gentleman as I have ever knowm. His advice to me since becoming a member of this house has been very valuable. He was a true Canadian and an example to all of us in his genuine love of Canada, and in his kindly tolerance of those of other views and of other religious and racial origins. He was beloved by all of us around him, whether Liberal or Conservative and whether English-speaking or French-speaking. I feel convinced that he had a great future before him in the public life of Canada, and it must be a matter of the deepest possible sorrow and regret that he was cut off so early in that career of service to his country. We deeply and sincerely sympathize with his family in their inexpressible loss and sorrow

speechtext:
Members of the house
will no doubt have seen the message which the President of the United States on Friday evening last communicated to the chancellor of the German Reich and to the chief of the Italian government. On Saturday evening the Charge d'Affaires of the United States legation officially communicated to me a copy of the message. Later in the evening I addressed a reply to the United States government in which I endeavoured to set forth what I believed would express the feeling of the Canadian people with reference to the message.
I should like to table the message of the president, and also the communication which
[Mr. Manion.J
I sent to the Charge d'Affaires, which was sent on to the Secretary of State at Washington and which has since been given out at Washington along with replies which have been received from other governments.
It is unnecessary for me to read the communications, but it might be of advantage if they were to be of record in Hansard as part of to-day's proceedings, and with the permission of the house I shall lay them on the table with a view to their being so recorded.

You realize I am sure that throughout the world hundreds of millions of human beings are living to-day in constant fear of a new war or even a series of wars. The existence of this fear-and the possibility of such a conflict-is of definite concern to the people of the United States for whom I speak, as it must also be to the peoples of the other nations of the entire western hemisphere. All of them know that any major war, even if it were to be confined to other continents, must bear heavily on them during its continuance and also for generations to come.
Because of the fact that after the acute tension in which the world has been living during the past few weeks there would seem to be at least a momentary relaxation-because no troops are at this moment on the march

this may be an opportune moment for me to send you this message.
On a previous occasion I have addressed you in behalf of the settlement of political, economic, and social problems by peaceful methods and without resort to arms.
But the tide of events seems to have reverted to the threat of arms. If such threats continue, it seems inevitable that much of the world must become involved in common ruin. All the world, victor nations, vanquished nations, and neutral nations will suffer. I refuse to believe that the world is, of necessity, such a prisoner of destiny. On the contrary, it is clear that the leaders of great nations have it in their power to liberate their peoples tfrom the disaster that impends. It is equally clear that in their own minds and in their own hearts the peoples themselves desire that their fears be ended. It is, however, unfortunately necessary to take cognizance of recent facts.
Three nations in Europe and one in Africa have seen their independent existence terminated. A vast territory- in another independent nation of the Far East has been occupied by a neighbouring state. Reports which we trust are not true, insist that further acts of aggression are contemplated against still other independent nations. Plainly the world is moving toward the moment when this situation must end in catastrophe unless a more rational way of guiding events is found.
You have repeatedly asserted that you and the German people have no desire for war. If this is true there need be no more.

European Situation
Nothing can persuade the peoples of the earth that any governing power has any right or need to inflict the consequences of war on its own or any other people save in the cause of self-evident home defence.
In making this statement we as Americans speak not through selfishness or fear or weakness. If we speak now it is with the voice of strength and with friendship for mankind. It is still clear to me that international problems can be solved at the council table.
It is therefore no answer to the plea for peaceful discussion for one side to plead that unless they receive assurances beforehand that the verdict will be theirs, they will not lay aside their arms. In conference rooms, as in courts, it is necessai'y that both sides enter upon the discussion in good faith, assuming that substantial justice will accrue to both; and it is customary and necessary that they leave their arms outside the room when they confer.
I am convinced that the cause of world peace would be greatly advanced if the nations of the world were to obtain a frank statement relating to the present and future policy of governments.
Because the United States, as one of the nations of the western hemisphere, is not involved in the immediate controversies which have risen in Europe, I trust that you may be willing to make such a statement of policy to me as the head of a nation far removed from Europe in order that I, acting only with the responsibility and obligation of a friendly intermediary, may communicate such declarations to other nations now apprehensive as to the course which the policy of your government may take.
Are you willing to give assurance that your armed forces will not attack or invade the territory or possessions of the following independent nations:	Finland, Estonia, Latvia,
Lithuania. Sweden, Norway, Denmark, The Netherlands, Belgium, Great Britain and Ireland, France, Portugal, Spain, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Luxemburg, Poland, Hungary, Roumania, Yugo-Slavia, Russia, Bulgaria, Greece, Turkey, Iraq, The Arabias, Syria, Palestine, Egypt and Iran.
Such an assurance clearly must apply not only to the present day but also to a future sufficiently long to give every opportunity to work by peaceful methods for a more permanent peace. I therefore suggest that you construe the word "future" to apply to a minimum period of assured non-aggression-ten years at the least-a quarter of a century, if we dare look that far ahead.
If such assurance is given by your government, I will immediately transmit it to the governments of the nations I have named and I will simultaneously inquire whether, as I am reasonably sure, each of the nations enumerated above will in turn give like assurance for transmission to you.
Reciprocal assurance such as I have outlined will bring to the world an immediate measure of relief.
I propose that if it is given, two essential problems shall promptly be discussed in the resulting peaceful surroundings, and in those discussions the government of the United States will gladly take part.
The discussions which I have in mind relate to the most effective and immediate manner through which the peoples of the world can obtain progressive relief from the crushing burden of armament which is each day bringing them more closely to the brink of economic
disaster. Simultaneously the government of the United States would be prepared to take part in discussions looking towards the most practical manner of opening up avenues of international trade to the end that every nation of the earth may be enabled to buy and sell on equal terms in the world market as well as to possess assurance of obtaining the materials and products of peaceful economic life.
At the same time, those governments other than the United States which are directly interested could undertake such political discussions as they may consider necessary or desirable.
We recognize complex world problems which affect all humanity but we know that study and discussion of them must be held in an atmosphere of peace. Such an atmosphere of peace cannot exist if negotiations are overshadowed by the threat of force or by the fear of war.
I think you will not misunderstand the spirit of frankness in which I send you this message. Heads of great governments in this hour are literally responsible for the fate of humanity in the coming years. They cannot fail to hear the prayers of their peoples to be protected from the foreseeable chaos of war. History will hold them accountable for the lives and the happiness of all-even unto the least.
I hope that your answer will make it possible for humanity to lose fear and regain security for many years to come.
A similar message is being addressed to the Chief of the Italian Government.

Statement by the Prime Minister of Canada, given to the Charge d'Affaires, United States Legation, Ottawa, upon receipt of a copy of President Roosevelt's address to the Chancellor of the German Reich and the Chief of the Italian Government.
Ottawa, April 15, 1939. At a moment of supreme concern, the president has acted with characteristic initiative and courage. His frank and realistic message is directed to the leaders and the peoples of two great European countries, but it is of vital interest to the people of every country. It gives the world a chance to halt on the brink of catastrophe.
The very fact that the danger is diffused, that there is no single issue, no one point of tension, has made it difficult to deal with the present situation. Now, the head of a great country, who appreciates what a conflict in Europe might come to mean to mankind, has brought the whole problem into sharp focus. He has presented an opportunity to all of sitting round a friendly table, where every grievance can be discussed frankly, and the readiness of each country, whether in Europe or outside it, to make its contribution to peaces and understanding, can be tested. In offering to join in the discussion of the disarmament and economic questions which lie at the root of so much of the world's unrest, the president has made a vital contribution in advance.
Mr. Roosevelt offers a peace conference before a war instead of after it. No country can lightly reject that opportunity of saving civilization and saving itself.
Canada welcomes the timely action of her good neighbour, and fervently hopes that it may meet with the response which the gravity of the situation demands.

DUNNING (Minister of Finance): Last week, in reply to a question put by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion), I intimated that I hoped to be able to bring down the budget on Thursday of this week. I now find that my hopes in that regard cannot be realized. In giving consideration to the matter, having regard also the desirability of expediting the business of the house, I may say it is now the definite intention to bring down the budget on Tuesday of next week.
I recognize, of course, that Tuesday is an unusual day, Thursday having the merit of permitting a week-end adjournment of the discussion in order that the opposition may have opportunity to study the document and all that it may imply; and for that reason I may say at once that the government will not object to any reasonable adjournment which may be requested following the budget speech.
I think I should also intimate to the house that it is the intention to try to follow this year, and possibly in future years, as the house may determine, the practice which is followed in Great Britain and also in Australia rf putting together what might be called the statistical and accounting information and ixplanations into one document, which is filed is a white paper and published as an appendix ;o the budget. This procedure will not only relieve me very greatly, but I am quite sure will relieve the house; since it will obviate the necessity of listening for quite a long period to figures and explanations of figures which it is quite impossible for anyone to carry in his mind and which in fact must be studied in their printed form before being used by any member in the course of debate or for any other purpose. I need not assure the house, I am certain, that the adoption of this procedure does not involve the giving of less information. Indeed, judging from my examination of the British and Australian records,
I think it may very well be a means of conveying more information than has been the practice in this house over a long period of years in connection with the 'budget, it being recognized that it is physically impossible to cover by means of the spoken word all the information which might reasonably be expected to be a part of the budget.
If, therefore, I have the consent of the house it is intended to adopt this procedure 
in the presentation of the budget this session. Of course it will be the right of the house in future to determine whether the procedure should be continued, in the light of the experience with it on this one occasion.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, April 14, consideration of the motion of Hon. Norman McL. Rogers (Minister of Labour) that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide assistance in the alleviation of
unemployment and agricultural distress and for such purpose to authorize the execution of undertakings in the general interest of Canada and requisite for the purposes of the act, out of moneys appropriated by parliament, and also to provide financial assistance to the provinces by way of loan, advance or guarantee, out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund, and for the appointment of necessary officers, clerks and employees.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I first decided to take part in the debate my mind was fully made up to deliver the most blistering denunciation of the government's policy that I could possibly make. But upon reflection it occurred to me that if I did adopt an attitude of that kind it would be rather selfish on my part, and that such a speech could not possibly contribute one iota to the solution of the problems we face to-day.
I also reflected upon one of the opening sentences in the speech of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey), when he said he felt like a ghoul about to feed on the fresh corpse of a dead debate. I listened carefully to his speech and realized that it consisted mostly of denunciation. I thought it would have been more appropriate if he had said, more truthfully, that he felt like a gladiator eager and anxious to thrust another stabbing and painful blow into the body of a defeated and beaten opponent. Because of his close association with the work of spreading the teachings of the Christian doctrine, the hon. member will realize perhaps better than anyone else the great truth of the suggestion I have made.
It occurred to me that such methods were selfish, inasmuch as they do not principally seek to help as much as they seek to secure political advantage. From time to time in the house ive hear hon. members from all sides say, "Let us forget party lines, and cooperate for the common good." Have we thought exactly what is meant by those words? They mean that we should drop our selfish attitude. We cannot cooperate with others until each of us has set his own house in order. For example, last Friday the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) himself was guilty of a little bit of selfishness when he denied that people in Canada had died of starvation and exposure, owing to lack of food and shelter.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend does not wish to misquote me. I did not deny that some had died. I denied the statement of the hon. member for Greenwood that thousands had died from such causes.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Perhaps the minister alters the statement he thought he made the other day.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: The hon. member will read Hansard and see my statement.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I am bound to accept the statement of the minister. Nevertheless the impression I got from his remarks and from the telegrams-I should say the gems- which were received from the various provincial governments was that nowhere in Canada could be found examples where people had died of exposure because of the lack of food, clothing or shelter. In order to have cooperation in this house, in order to forget party lines, we should begin with ourselves. I realize, of course, that the minister could not admit that such a thing could happen in this country. That would have meant his job; it would have hurt his political colleagues and done damage to his political affiliations. The minister read a telegram in this house from Mr. A. MacNamara, who is I understand deputy minister of labour in the province of Manitoba. It is to be found on page 2785 of Hansard of Friday, April 14, and reads in part as follows:
There have been no cases of death due to malnutrition, starvation or exposure attributable to lack of sufficiency, inavailability or amount of relief in Manitoba during the last four 5rears.
At the very moment the minister was standing up in this house reading this gem from the province of Manitoba, we found this article in the press:
Winnipeg, April 13.-The body of an unidentified man, believed a transient, was found to-day in an old coach in the Canadian Pacific railway yards here. Death was believed due to exposure and starvation.
This man had died and had been found in an old coach just the day before that telegram left Winnipeg. That is why I say that the minister or the official handling relief in Winnipeg could not admit that such things were taking place in Canada. The minister knows just as well as I that this is not the only case. He has himself read reports time and time again in Canadian newspapers describing happenings such as this. I admit at once that such items do not receive much prominence. I found this one buried on page thirteen of one of our local newspapers, just underneath the social column. The things most prominently displayed on that page are occurrences such as teas given by the Prime Minister. When a transient dies in an old coach, the report does not receive much prominence. As a matter of fact, the officials 
of that province did not think it necessary to tell the minister of what had happened just the day before the telegram was sent.
I turn now to another gem sent by an official in the province of Alberta who signs himself A. A. Mackenzie, commissioner of relief and public welfare. I venture to say at once that the government of Alberta was not aware that such a communication was sent to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). He refers in his telegram to the fifty cent bonus which the relief recipients received at Christmas and the statement is made that in most cases this money was expended extravagantly. All they received was fifty cents per capita with which to buy a Packard car, I suppose, or other things which they could not otherwise afford to buy. This official goes on to state:
Persons making such statements should be made produce evidence or action taken to prevent such prevarication in the future.
That gentleman should be made to prove that the people on relief in his province are just as healthy as the wealthier families. I mention these two examples simply because they are outstanding. While I hesitate to use the term, it seems to me that the facts are a direct lie to this statement. This transient was found in an old coach, dead from starvation and exposure. It happened the day before the minister made his statement. I am wondering just what happened in Manitoba. Did the official deliberately keep from the minister certain information which he must have had as to this occurrence? I quote these two gems, as I desire to call them, not because they happen to be typical of the provinces of Alberta and Manitoba, but because they are the two most outstanding examples at my disposal at the moment. I feel quite sure that similar things have occurred in other provinces of Canada.
The transient problem is not a problem belonging to one or two provinces; it affects the whole of the dominion. For fear that it might be said that this is the only example I could find, I should like to refer to another incident which occurred some time ago. It has to do with a transient who used to live on the Ottawa East dump-I ask every hon. member to note the address of this man. The report states that a train moving out of Ottawa struck a man described as Tony Mazuerko, aged sixty-six years, a transient who had been living on the Ottawa East dump. The report states further that apparently the man had not had sufficient food, the result being that he did not have enough strength to hang on to the box car when he

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
tried to climb on board. Exactly one week later, we find this report of an occurrence right in the shadow of this peace tower:
A week or so ago, city police found another so-called transient almost frozen to death in an empty garage. The report said he had collapsed because of "malnutrition," in other words, in a state of starvation.
Every hon. member of this house could go on reading reports of incidents like this the whole day long. This is not an isolated case, it is simply an example of what other hon. members must know.
I should like to refer to the situation which exists in Sorel, in the province of Quebec, and read a letter which I have received from that part of the country. This shows that the unemployment problem is widespread in scope and does not belong to only one part of the country. The letter is in French, and I shall read it in that language. It reads:
(Translation) Some of them are on relief, others are being assisted by means of public collections, and the remainder are just tightening their belts. We have taken all possible means to obtain assistance from the Ottawa government, but in vain. The city of Sorel has reached the limit of its borrowing capacity and the province has done all it could. Had the province not come to our assistance, many people would have starved to death by this time. . . .
In February last, when the people were about to make a slight demonstration to show their need of food, twenty detectives came on the scene, but after inquiry they decided in favour of the demonstrators. If the government does not help us, I do not know what will happen. Although we are opposed to communism, we are not going to let our children starve. The federal government should come to our assistance as soon as possible.

Instead of placing it on the record I shall relate the conditions that exist in the city of Sorel as I know them of my own personal knowledge. Because of certain transactions which took place not long ago, a large number of people became unemployed in Sorel. I have been informed that many hundreds of these people have had to go about the town begging from door to door in order to secure food for themselves. I can quite believe that, in view of the fact that not very long ago exactly the same thing happened in the town of Aylmer, close to this city of Ottawa.
Here is another example which is very much in point. It is case No. 127, taken from a report of case histories by Jean Graham Low, appearing in the Ottawa Citizen of Saturday, April 15, 1939:
This family is having tough sledding. During the time the father works, and is being budgeted, until they become eligible for relief again it seems to be starvation and no halfmeasures. There are seven children in this instance whose ages range as follows: three boys, 18-15-11; four girls, 13-8J-6-3 years. All of these children need clothes in the worst way, especially the three bo3's. Families w-ho are supposed to live in a similar state when employed as they would if they were receiving relief are to be sympathized with. When they are on relief, no back bills can be paid, and no one bothers them too much. Yet, when the man gets employment everyone to whom he owes money is after him, hotfoot. If he does not pay, his wages are garnisheed, and if he does pay, he simply cannot save. When he is penniless and applies for relief he is told that his earnings should have done him a certain length of time. The fact of his having bills to pay, as well as current living expenses, does not enter into his favour at all and the whole family starve during the "waiting period" until they are reinstated with the relief again, providing no earnings have been made meanwhile. The woman
2846	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
came to me and cried bitterly. She said, "We haven't a bite to eat for supper, I'm telling you the truth and you can believe me. Our relief does not come due until early in May. What we are to do from this, until that date, I don't know."
Simply another case, and, again, one not very far away, but in the very shadow of the peace tower. Yet the minister tells us that there is no such thing in this country as death caused !by starvation. I am sure that if we are to eliminate selfishness and bring about closer cooperation, forgetting party divisions, we must all first begin with ourselves. If we do that we shall make better and faster headway.
When the minister made his statement in the house on January 23 last he referred to the action taken by his party in securing foreign markets and thereby increasing private employment. I intend to refer to this, not in a critical manner, but simply to buttress the argument I am making to prove that under the present financial set-up the minister cannot hope to do more than anyone else in his place could do. I took the trouble to compare the amounts of our favourable trade balances in certain recent years with the number of people in receipt of assistance in the same periods. These records are taken from reports issued by the present government. In 1933, when Canada's favourable balance of trade was S128,500,000, one and a half million people were receiving assistance. In the following year Canada's favourable balance of trade was $238,250,000, with 1,349,000 people on relief. In 1937, which was the year of our greatest favourable trade balance, amounting to $402,000,000, the number of persons receiving assistance in one form or another was still as high as 1,215,000. So that even though we succeeded in increasing in a large measure our favourable balance of trade, that achievement has not been reflected in a decrease in the number of persons receiving assistance from the government. It seems to me, therefore, that it is logical and timely that we should abandon this idea that it is necessary for us to feed everybody else in order to be able to provide our own people with food, clothing and shelter.
Another proposition which is made to us is that we should spend sufficient money on public works, such as road construction, to lift ourselves out of the so-called depression. We are told that if we adopt that kind of program we can provide employment for practically all our people. That might be the result for a time; as a matter of fact I have no objection to spending large sums of money

on public works, because I am convinced that in any case the principal of our national debt will never be repaid. But to say that such a course will provide a solution of our problem is to my mind the height of folly. We could not have a better example of the results of any such action than the experience of the program entered upon and carried on by our southern neighbours. To use a term which is often used in slang, the people of the United States "went after it in a big way." In the last ton years they spent over twenty-five billion dollars in trying to get back to prosperity. But what do the figures show? In 1929 in the United States there were 469,000 people unemployed. Ten years later, after spending about twenty-five billion dollars, there are 10,981.000 unemployed. Yet no nation ever went to work and spent money on public works on a larger scale than did our neighbours to the south. It could be truthfully said that the United States spent more money to find recovery and found less recovery than any other nation in the world. I do not say this because I believe that it should not have been done. Of course it should have been done. The only thing wrong was that they borrowed money to do it, just as we propose to do, and at the end of a decade of effort they have succeeded in adding to their national obligations a fixed debt charge of one billion dollars per year. The result necessarily must be an increase in taxation. No permanent cure of unemployment has yet been found. It cannot be found through the present system, and the fact might as well be admitted.
I could go on and quote tables taken from a volume which I commend to every hon. member. It is a publication issued by Robert L. Owen, former chairman of the committee on banking and currency, United States senate. The figures I have just quoted are taken from a report of the National Industrial Conference Board, Inc., of New York city, which keeps a record of unemployment in the United States. The publication goes on to show, as I have said, that the only thing they have learned from their experiment is that by issuing a large amount of money they can reduce slightly, for a short period of time, the number of people unemployed. The reason there was no great success in the United States is simply that they continued under the old orthodox system of trying to get out of a depression by financing production instead of financing the consumer. However, I believe that they are learning the lesson, because since that time I have read an article from the Washington

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
bureau of the Wall Street Journal referring to a plan given out by the government, as follows:
A plan to dispose of surplus production will he put into operation about April the first this year. It will affect more than twenty million people. The aim is to give "purchase certificates"-
I underline ' the word "give."
-in addition to present relief cheques. The United States Department of Agriculture plans to distribute surplus agricultural products to the needy through regular retail channels by the use of these free purchase certificates in addition to all other forms of purchasing power now available.
They are doing something there which we in the province of Alberta have attempted to do. We tried to put this plan into operation in that province, but for certain reasons well known to most hon. members we have not been able to do so as completely as we desired. However, we have begun, and I believe that the record of the province of Alberta is better than that of any other province. In the last three years Alberta has gone ahead faster than any other province. At one time the amount of building contracts in Alberta was greater in value than those of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia combined. During that time our industries have been developed in that province to an unprecedented extent, and in addition to that we have initiated the greatest campaign of buying made-in-Alberta goods that this dominion has ever known. That is why the government of Alberta are in a position to say that conditions in that province have been better since they came into power than they ever had been before. I say this because we have been criticized for failure in that province to keep the unemployment problem under control, on the ground that it comes within the jurisdiction of this parliament alone. However, I do not think it can be denied that the province of Alberta can show a better record than any other part of the dominion. Let me read from a pamphlet, Now There's Treasury Branch Service in Your Own Home Town, to show what has been accomplished in Alberta, after many obstacles have been overcome. This pamphlet sets out "seven good reasons why you should make sure that you get all the benefits of treasury branch service." Let me quote one or two of these reasons:
1. Every time you spend a dollar by using transfer vouchers you get a bonus of three cents, provided at least one-third of your purchases were " Alberta-made."
2.	Your money or transfer voucher deposits earn two per cent or more interest for you when you deposit them in a treasury branch savings account.
I will leave out the other reasons. Number 7 reads:
7. As your use of the treasury branches helps to bring about their success, it will become increasingly possible to issue credit in terms of the needs of the people, and Alberta will go marching forward into a new era of plenty, in which everyone will share.
At least they have recognized that until credit is issued in terms of public need, no progress can be made. This government seemed to suggest the same thing prior to 1935, but their attitude at that time is now something that belongs to the dim and distant past. They forget what they said in those days and now we find they have taken the entirely opposite attitude.
There was a report in one of the newspapers on April 1. 1939, to the effect that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had been reliably reported to have told his caucus that it was useless to ask him, on behalf of the Liberal party, to try to end unemployment, because it could not be done. I submit that he was quite right when he said it could not be done, but he should have added "under the present economic system." I have no doubt that was what he meant, but he should have added those words, because it certainly cannot be done under the present system. After all, the proof is there; the record is there.
I am quite sure both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour wish to solve the problem if it can possibly be done. I am willing to concede that they earnestly desire to do what they can for the country, and I believe the record will show that they have taken every possible step within the limits of the system they follow to bring about the end they have in view. When the Prime Minister decided that he would solve the problem, what did he do? He got the best brains he could possibly find within the ranks of the Liberal party. For example, he got the present Minister of Labour. Let me read the minister's record, giving his degrees. I quote:
Rogers. Hon. Norman McLeod, B.A., M.A., B.Litt., B.C.L., (Kingston City, Ont.) .	.	.
Educated at Cumberland county academy, Acadia university and Oxford university.

Has written many articles for periodicals on economic and constitutional questions. In 1934 served as counsel for Nova Scotia government before royal commission of economic inquiry.
With such admirable academic training, and with such an organization behind him, the Minister of Labour has failed to solve the problem; and if he cannot do it, I ask in all sincerity, on behalf of the people who are asking the same question, how the government can hope to do it. If this gentleman, with such brains, cannot find a solution under the present economic system, who else will solve the problem?

speechtext: Now you are talking. He has tried to solve it, and he has really found the fundamental cause of the trouble. That cause lies in the present faulty monetary system of the country, and that is what we in this corner have been trying to bring home to the house ever since we came to parliament.

speechtext: Why doesn't he pay his debts?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Your party goes deeper into debt. We are all on relief in this house, trying to pay our way out of our indemnity, but that is not true of all members, because some happen to be in a more fortunate position. However, that is by the way. We are discussing matters affecting the government. I would ask hon. gentlemen opposite to tell me when the public debt of Canada has ever been reduced. When have we ever paid anything on the principal? On very few occasions since confederation; and to-day the trend is to go into debt with accelerating speed.
However, I was discussing the qualifications of the Minister of Labour, and I say that with his splendid record, with the able assistance he has had and the powerful organization behind him, he has failed, and it is no wonder the Prime Minister gets up in his own caucus and says, "I do not believe that I should be expected to declare that this party can solve the unemployment problem to-day." I do not say that critically. I am not criticizing the government at all. AVhy should I criticize them? I think they ought to be commended for fighting to the last ditch to bring about some improvement under the present system. But it cannot be done under that system.
The Conservatives hope to become the next government, but that is doubtful accord-

ing to a statement made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) in London the other day. They also had one of the most brilliant men in the country as leader of their party-I refer to the last leader. Undoubtedly the present leader is an equally brilliant man, and the Conservatives also have a powerful organization. They get up and tell us about their eleven-point program, but they forget to ask themselves where the money is to come from. What is the good of their talking about carrying on public works, providing old age pensions at a lower age limit, and so on? We are all agreed that these things should be done, but the Conservatives should tell us the one thing which apparently they have forgotten, namely, how these ends can be achieved under the present economic system. We in Alberta have tried honestly and sincerely to get at the problem by understanding its fundamentals. We have realized that it is control of credit and currency that really counts. We are not blind to the possibilities of Canada, to the natural resources of the country, nor are we blind to the needs of the poor, and therefore we want to inaugurate the monetary policy which will serve to distribute the wealth of Canada to those who need it.
If the Minister of Labour did not regard the present system as hopeless, he would tell us why it was that, when he knew that there were vegetables rotting in the southern part of Ontario, there were at the same time people suffering from scurvy in the northern section of the province. Of course he will say it is a provincial question, that we have nothing to do with it. But it was this government who told the people that they would end unemployment; they were going to make this question one of national concern. Now I am beginning to believe that it was mostly because of his familiarity with the constitutional question that the present Minister of Labour was put into that position. He has shown a great deal of ability in getting'around these questions by hiding behind constitutional points. Undoubtedly there may be some grounds for his acting in that manner. I can only say that although they have at their command the very best brains and unlimited money, hon. gentlemen admit that they have failed. That is the greatest condemnation of the present economic system that we could possibly have, the greatest demonstration possible in any country of how useless it is to try to tax yourself out of depression and bring back prosperity, or to borrow yourself out of debt. It is not by a program involving the expenditure of $150,000,000 or $100,000,000 on public

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
works that we are going to get anywhere. For the time being it might help; it might help certain local interests, but it is not solving the problem. And with this admitted failure to solve the problem the time has come when this country must look to someone else to take hold and solve it.
I had intended to refer, but my time is getting short, to the back to the land movement. We were told the other day by the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) that a nephew of his-he let us in on one of his family secrets-had refused to go back to the land, although he was offered every possible attraction. All I can say is that the people on the farms do not object to being on the farms; what they do object to is that there is nothing in it for them. That is the cause of all their misery. They do not object to working from dawn until sundown, provided that they are able to secure a living by doing so.
Any attempt to solve the problem of unemployment under our present economic set-up has been proved futile by the present administration. Everything that could be desired was at their disposal-brains, organization, money; yet the situation to-day is just as bad as it ever was. There are just as many people receiving assistance now as there were some time ago. Except in the middle of the summer, the number never goes much below a million. Why not come out and say in a straightforward way that there is no solution under the present economic system? We have tried everything; we have the example of the United States of America; we know that foreign markets are becoming more and more restricted, that nations which formerly were importing nations have now adopted a policy of national self-sufficiency. But that is beside the point; for I cannot agree that it is necessary first to feed the world in order to be able to feed the people who are starving within our own land.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
First I wish to congratulate the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) on his statement in regard to youth training and youth employment. I know the deep and sincere interest he has in these subjects. He has strongly advocated youth training, and he realizes to the fullest extent the urgent need of employment for youth.
A few weeks ago I had the privilege of introducing to him representatives of the service clubs of Canada. At that meeting delegates representing Rotary, Gyro, Progress, Kiwanis, Optimists, Kinsmen, Lions and
Civitan organizations were present and testified to their personal desire and the willingness of the clubs they represented to cooperate with the government in any plan or plans for the employment of the youth of our country. I am glad that the government have shown their interest in forest conservation by referring to it specifically in the speech from the throne, in the words following:
As a means of providing an opportunity for useful work and national service to single unemployed men, the assistance given to forest conservation will be extended to include other work of national importance.
The beneficial results of the youth training program have demonstrated the wisdom of this experiment, and a measure wTiIl be introduced to increase its efficiency and expand its usefulness.
I am glad to see on the order paper the resolution which we are now discussing, and also Bill No. 94, to provide for the training of young people to fit them for gainful employment.
It is well that in considering this question of forest conservation we should have in mind the original state of many parts of Canada, particularly some parts of the province of Ontario, with which I am most familiar, observe what has happened over a period of years, and consider what steps can be taken to improve conditions.
Our forefathers claimed the land from the forests and laid the foundations of rural communities in the farming districts now in existence. At that time the forests were a great help to them in augmenting their food supply with fish and fowl and in providing building material for their farm buildings. But the pioneers had the problem of clearing sufficient land to raise crops to feed themselves and supply pasture and feed for their live stock. In those early days the forests seemed a veritable enemy which they had to conquer in order to exist. In many districts no market was available for the timber, and if there had been a market, there were no transportation facilities to enable them to reach it. As a result logs were piled and burnt in order to get the land cleared for the planting of crops. Throughout the years more and more timber has been cut, more and more land turned into pasture, and as time and opportunity permitted the stumps were pulled and the land brought under cultivation When the land was originally cleared it was very fertile and provided homes for many settlers, and as transportation facilities were improved there was a large influx of people.
For many years in those areas substantial woodlots and stands of valuable timber remained on the farms. But in recent years
2850	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
many of the timber stands have disappeared and a substantial proportion of the woodlots are being used for grazing-in fact are being overgrazed, thus preventing the growth of new trees.
Through the interest and financial support of Mr. Aubrey Davis, of Newmarket, Ontario, there was made possible the carrying out of a comprehensive survey of general conditions in the township of King during the last two years. Mr. K. A. Mayall, a graduate forester, was in charge of the staff which carried out this work. He had the benefit of the advice of a board of which Professor W. J. K. Harkness, of the department of biology, of the university of Toronto was chairman, and received the cooperation of the council of the township of King and a committee of representative citizens of that district. In view of the accurate and detailed information resulting from that survey, I wish to take that township as an example of existing conditions.
The township of King, with an area of nearly 140 square miles, is situated about twenty miles north and northwest of Toronto. Most of the township is rolling or hilly country, with a well-marked divide running across its centre from east to west. This ridge is the height of land between lake Ontario and lake Simcoe. The altitude varies from a minimum of about 670 feet on the banks of the Humber to more than 1,200 feet on the height of land. The normal precipitation in that district is about 28-94 inches and the average snowfall about 4 feet.
The peak of population in this township was reached about 1871, when it had a population of 7,500. By that time almost all the available farming land was cleared and cultivated The falling off of the local industries in the ten villages of the township has caused a steady drop in the population, which in 1936 was listed as 4,636. The population of King township is widely scattered and concerned almost exclusively with mixed farming, oats and wheat being the commonest grain crops, while practically every farm has a herd of dairy cattle. The sole remnant of the former industrial activity of the township is a planing mill at Schomberg. There are three remaining grist mills, but none of these now use water power.
In that township the percentage of wooded land required to maintain a sufficient water supply for farm use and to ensure soil conservation and wild life shelter varies according to soil type, climate, the slope of the land, the method of cultivation and the species of trees involved. In rolling land, such as the township of King, there is no doubt that at least fifteen per cent of well spaced, ungrazed
[Mr. MulockJ
woods is essential. In this township there are now only 4,042 acres or 4-9 per cent of the township in ungrazed woods. A further 4,499 acres of land is covered with woods or pastures in which overgrazing has left little or no young growth. Such woods are no longer sufficient in water-holding capacity. They supply no consistent yield of fuel to the farmers, and they provide little or no protection for wild life. The addition of the grazed woods to the present ungrazed woods in the township would only raise the percentage of all types of cover in that area to 10-4 per cent. The results of the survey of water conditions and soil erosion show that this percentage is inadequate to keep the land in stable condition for the greatest benefit of its inhabitants. Almost all the wood lots in King township are seriously understocked. The Dominion Fuel Board report states in part:
Not over ten per cent of all classes of wood-lots are producing within fifty per cent of the possible annual increment in wood volume per acre.
It is improbable that the average growth exceeds -6 cords per acre per annum. No data are available on the possible growth in well managed mixed woodlots in Ontario handled on the basis of sustained yield; but the hardwood forests of the Michigan Agricultural College have been yielding at the rate of 1-2 cords per acre per annum without reducing the growing stock. At this rate, if well managed, ungrazed and replanted in part, the 8,500 acres of wood in King township would produce more than 10,000 cords per annum without reducing the growing stock, instead of the present probable growth of about 5,000 cords per annum with a continual drop in the growing stock from woodlands ruined by overgrazing.
Of the two hundred miles of permanent streams which formerly drained the township only about thirty miles now remain. As an example, Hall's lake stream, which formerly supplied a permanent flow of water on which two factories and six mills depended, was dry in 1936. Twenty-eight mill ponds which formerly held a constant supply of water are now reduced to one pond. The mill ponds, with the permanent lakes and natural ponds formerly existing, made up more than five hundred acres of water surface apart from the rivers. The present permanent water surface in King township, exclusive of rivers or canals, is less than two hundred acres. The bureau of geology and topography of the Department of Mines and Resources carried out a ground water survey during 1937 which included this township. Of 1,572 wells in the township examined during the course of the

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
survey, 264 no longer can be relied upon to supply a permanent flow of water; and 72 others, while permanent, no longer supply enough water for the needs of the farmers concerned. These facts can lead to only one conclusion, that the ground water, or reserve of water supplying springs and wells, has been seriously lowered since the main woodlands in the township were cut. It is interesting to note that the four permanent streams now draining the township all have their origin in areas of ungrazed woodland. Coincident with the lowering of the ground water level there has been a noticeable increase in the number and severity of both spring and summer floods. The present trends in regard to the water reserves in the township are very low, and it can be forecast that further depletion of woodlots will lead to a further lowering of the ground water, with consequent drying up of springs and streams.
Both sheet and gully erosion are now very common in the township. The most spectacular form of erosion is the formation of gullies, but economically it is the loss of the topsoil which has caused the abandonment of many farm lands which never should have been cleared. All these lands are either too sandy or too steep to give any hope of sustained yield under cultivation. They are admirably suited to the growing of trees, however.
So far as this township is concerned the proper course to follow would be to release the present grazed woods from grazing and to replant some of the overgrazed woodlots, which would raise the percentage to 10-4. The further addition of 4,250 acres of plantation would bring the total woodlots in the township to 15-6 per cent, or within the margin of safety. In addition several small dams should be reconstructed near the headwaters of certain streams and the Schomberg and Kettleby dams should be repaired. The Schomberg dam drains an area of about eleven square miles and the Kettleby dam an area of about eight square miles. These dams will serve to reduce floods and soil erosion. They will make available a constant flow of water for stream improvement; they will aid in raising the ground water level, and their ponds will improve conditions for wild life.
More than 2,500 acres of former farm lands are now cleared but no longer cultivated. On practically every farm there are two or three acres of waste land, and exclusive of the Holland marsh it is estimated that there are at least
17,000	acres of land in the township not adapted to profitable farming. The project therefore appears practical if it receives the cooperation of the farmers.
In this connection I might mention that during the 1937 survey of the natural resources of King township more than 700 acres of land were made available by farmers for the immediate planting of trees.
The province of Ontario has made a substantial start on the work of reforestation, and a similar effort has been made in the province of Quebec though not on such a large scale. So far as Ontario is concerned this work was commenced in 1905 but was substantially increased in 1922 by the establishment of two additional nurseries, one at Orono in Durham county and the other at Midhurst in Sim-coe county. Since 1924, when these two nurseries commenced to distribute planting material, the annual output has increased from 1,000,000 to 22,000,000 for 1939. Until 1922 the distribution of trees was chiefly for planting on privately owned land, for supplementing existing farm woodlots and for windbreak planting for agricultural purposes. At that time the number of persons receiving trees was a few hundred, while in 1938 the number had reached 8,000.
The county forest system, which provides for a county buying thousand-acre tracts of waste land and having these managed under an agreement with the Department of Lands and Forests of the provincial government, for a period of thirty years, was commenced in 1922. At the present time there are sixteen of these forests in operation by twelve counties, with a total acreage of 18,227. In addition the province carries on inspection of farmers' wood lots. Advice is given to prospective planters and extensive educational work is carried on by means of lectures to service clubs, agricultural short courses, and other groups.
Let us consider the shift in population from the rural districts to the cities in Ontario. I have dealt with the population of the township of King, which reached its peak about 1871, when the population stood at 7,500. In 1936 it had fallen to 4,636. But that condition is not restricted to any one township. Let us consider the figures for the county of Bruce. In 1901 the population stood at 59,020. In 1933 it had dropped to 42,066, a loss of almost 17,000 people in a period of thirty-two years. No doubt some of those people went to western Canada, but it is also true that many moved into our cities. I have given the figures for the county of Bruce, as an example, but I might point out that nineteen counties in Ontario with large areas of non-agricultural land showed decreases in total population.
2852	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
The extensive cutting of trees, without proper replacement, has, I submit, brought about or contributed to the following conditions, not only in Ontario but in many other provinces:
1.	Insufficient protection of springs and creeks. In farming districts springs are disappearing and wells are drying up, and farmers have to drive their herds long distances to water, or haul water in barrels.
2.	The rushing of water in flood times causes the top soil to be gradually carried away, with the result that soil erosion is becoming prevalent in our eastern provinces.
3.	The lack of protection in the form of forests and substantial woodlots which tend to hold moisture has substantially contributed to the causing of floods which have caused injury and loss of life, and a tremendous amount of property damage.
We do not need to look to our friends to the south to see what floods mean. We have them in Ontario. For instance, one need only point to the damage done by floods in the Grand valley area in 1937 and the loss occasioned to the people of London. We have had floods at Port Hope and Belleville, points lying farther to the east, as well as in many other places in the province. We have reduced the flow in our rivers to a point where, from the health standpoint, their summer levels are positively dangerous. It has seriously affected our water supply. From year to year the fish and game situation has gone from bad to worse, and precipitation in the form of rain has steadily dropped because of the denuding of our land.
Our western provinces have suffered from drought condition, soil drift and soil erosion. We have an example of the useful work which this government has carried out under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, as proof that the construction of conservation works and reforestation is not an experiment but is a successful and proven fact. We have also as an example of its success the civilian conservation corps camps under the "new deal" program, put in operation by the government of the United States. It is generally agreed that the civilian conservation corps camps are by far the most successful of the relief measures adopted by the Roosevelt administration. Those camps were the first large-scale effort made by the United States government to bring definite physical and character benefits to its idle youth. They furnish employment annually to an aggregate number of about
450,000	young men, 50,000 war veterans and approximately 35,000 reserve officers. The maximum number in camps at any one time
	.
is about 300,000. Under this scheme more than two million young men and war veterans have found new opportunity in life. Useful construction works have been built, reforestation and conservation have and are being carried on, and the wealth of the nation is being built up.
Selection is made under uniform national standards of eligibility. These standards relate to age, citizenship, unemployment and relief status, marital status, character and physical fitness. As a condition precedent to enrolment each junior enrollee must agree to allot to a dependent relative a substantial portion of his monthly pay of $30. The man's family thus receives each month, directly from the finance office, an allotment cheque of from $22 to $25 to be used in meeting family needs.
I suggest the government should cooperate to the fullest extent with the provinces to bring this scheme into operation, not only to assist in the extension of the existing forestry work, but also, through a substantial enlargement of the program, to encourage construction work for conservation purposes. I would say that the federal ministers charged with the administration of this work and the responsibility for its success should, in cooperation with the provinces, consider making regulations to deal with the following:
1.	A form of education dealing with schoolyard planting of trees, to bring home to our young people the necessity of reforestation and conservation, and to impress upon them that it is in their own personal interests and in the interests of Canada.	.
2.	The replanting of areas on which timber has been cut.
3.	The clearing of slash.
4.	Controlling the location, size and quantity of timber to be cut.
5.	Controlling the wasteful cutting of young trees on lands planted under this plan.
The thinning out process will provide a substantial revenue and help to reduce operating expenses. According to a press release dated April 13, 1939, the government has decided it will set aside a million dollars for a national forestry program, as an extension of the youth training plan. This is a good start. It is estimated that at least 4,000 young men will be assisted during a period of about five months. I hope the government will consider extending the plan to larger proportions.
A program similar to that in operation in the civilian conservation corps camps, carried out in cooperation with the provinces, would,
I believe, have the active support of the provincial governments, county councils,

municipal authorities and large numbers of the Canadian people. We could do much to help the country. In the first place, we can assist our farmers by preventing soil erosion and ensuring soil conservation. We can preserve the natural water supply in wells and springs which now exist, and by a carefully planned program we can restore water where wells and springs are drying up. By replanting we can increase the value of the farms, and give to the farmers a steady yield of fuel. We can restore our fishing and wild life, which is of the greatest importance to the tourist business in Canada, and on which our federal government spends large sums annually for advertising purposes.
These conservation works regulating the flow from swampy districts and forming lakes in which the levels can be controlled, will substantially reduce spring and summer floods and create a more uniform flow of water in our streams and rivers throughout the year. We will be building up the wealth of Canada. When the money has been expended on these works, we shall have something definite and substantial to show in increased national wealth. In the northern parts of some of the provinces tremendous areas of our forests have been cut with the slash left on the ground. Apart from ruining the appearance of the country and ending fish and wild life, this has created a very serious fire hazard. We will be assisting in providing more work throughout the country. Such a scheme would encourage and assist many people to return to the country from the cities. Many of these people were unable to make a living on their farms or obtain gainful employment under existing conditions. It might be well for us to recall the remarks made by President Roosevelt when addressing the people of his country. He said:
You have felt the rough hand of the depression. You have walked the streets looking for jobs that never turn up. Out of this has come physical hardships and more serious scare of disillusionment. The temper of our youth has become more restless, more critical, more challenging. Flaming youth has become a flaming question.
In other -words, he said that our youth want an opportunity to make an honest living and a reasonable chance to improve their conditions in life as they grow older. They want practical assurance against want in old age, and with it the right to enjoy the finer things of life.
I believe in the enlargement of the present scheme and I wish to congratulate the government on making this start. I hope it is a start by which we will be able to give useful employment to thousands of our young people and replace the despair which is now in their hearts with well-founded confidence in their future and the future of this country.
