speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his remarks on the unemployment insurance resolution, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) expressed the view that industry should recognize its responsibility and obligation to assist in the movement for the relief of unemployment. With the minister's view there was common accord. A few days later, during the discussion on the Canada-United States trade treaty, reference was made to the fact that certain industries in Canada were being jeopardized because the treaty permitted the entry into Canada of the mass production output of United States industries to compete with Canadian plants producing similar products. It is obvious that when you reduce production, you also reduce employment and increase relief. I believe that industry recognizes its obligation and is willing to cooperate with the government, but it does feel discouraged with the heavy taxation it has to bear and with the legislative enactments which have to do with its operations.
The present government and its predecessor have proceeded on the assumption that unemployment conditions were only temporary and that each succeeding year would show an improvement. Such measures as have been brought in for relief have been temporary in character. However, the government should be willing to receive suggestions from industry, even though some of those suggestions may be somewhat radical in character. The time has come when the government mtist cooperate more closely with industry. I believe we shall have to adopt the five-day week. If there is one example of the working of the law of supply and demand it is to be found in our present condition of an excess number of workers with a scarcity of jobs.
In my district we have a good example of what can result from the introduction of the five-day week. There are about 5,000 employees in the plant there, and when the depression came along it was a question of either reducing the hours of labour or laying off a great many men. The employees [DOT] chose to adopt the five-day week rather than have certain of their numbers lose their pay cheques entirely. When conditions improved the employees were given an opportunity to
2854 _	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
Bay whether they wanted to continue with the five-day week or go back to the six-day week. They chose the five-day week. The result has been that these men have had time for a little recreation; they have been able to improve their homes and gardens, and they are well satisfied. I think the government might consider conferring with labour organizations throughout the country with a view to ascertaining the opinion of labour generally and of industry with regard to accepting a shortening of the hours of work. This would certainly give employment to a great many people throughout the dominion. The bureau of statistics have figures to show that if the five-day week which has been adopted at Trail were adopted generally throughout the country, it would mean that 150,000 unemployed would be given employment.
I come now to a matter which I think should appeal to the government, that is, the apprenticeship system. The industry at Trail has a program by which the sons of employees are registered as apprentices. They are taken on at a fair wage rate, which is increased periodically. When they have served their time and become journeymen, if there is no vacancy in the particular department in which they have served their apprenticeship, employment is found for them in some other department until a vacancy occurs in which they can pursue the line of work for which they have been trained. There is also a training instructor who gives them four hours a week technical instruction. I do'not think there is anything which can contribute so much to the welfare of a young man as an apprenticeship service. I note from a release in the press that the Minister of Labour suggests that there shall be a training camp for air pilots, air mechanics and others; I know of nothing which would be more attractive to our young men.
In South Africa they have a regular apprenticeship system. Young men are registered legally for apprenticeship in various vocations, and in the past five years
12.000	young men have been registered for four and a half year apprenticeships, so that they will become skilled workmen, able to take their place in the industrial life of the country. The South African government has also a system for the training of youths from seventeen to twenty-two years of age in what is called a service battalion. These young men must be physically and mentally fit. Special educational qualifications are required. They receive daily training, and the government constitutes Itself an employment agency to find for them suitable positions in life. There
is also what is known as a pioneer battalion, consisting of men without special educational qualifications, but who are trained and well provided for and are used largely in the construction of public works. The government of South Africa takes the view that modern apprenticeship must have a place in the educational system of a nation, because it is the one and only sound way of training skilled workers.
I wish to refer also to the generous sum appropriated for the purpose of encouraging tourist travel in Canada, which is such an important asset. At the last session the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) referred to the construction of highways for tourist use,-and there is no greater attraction to the tourist than that of good roads. Paved highways over the state of Washington bring to British Columbia tourists from eastern Washington, Idaho, Oregon and various parts of the Pacific coast. They come here over hard-surfaced standard highways, but when they get to the section of British Columbia known as the Kootenays they find two highways connecting with the transprovincial highway, and both in a most deplorable condition. There is one which comes into Nelson, the capital of the Kootenays, from the international line at Nelway; another one joins the transprovincial highway at Rossland. This transprovincial highway is the only highway by which you can get from Vancouver to Lake Louise and Banff, and I ask the Minister of Mines and Resources to give consideration to the necessity of cooperating with the provincial government a.nd securing the improvement of those two highways.
What I wanted to speak about chiefly was the mining situation in what is known as the Silvery Slocan. For many years that mining section of the interior of British Columbia has produced a great deal of silver, lead and zinc. To-day the silver properties are idle and many of them which started production last year have found it necessary to cease operations because of the low price of silver. In the United States, as hon. members know, the government has a price of 64-4 cents per ounce for silver newly mined within the United States. That price they have extended for a period of two years. The various boards of trade in this silver district of West Kootenay have presented to the government resolutions asking that the government pay sixty-five cents or 64-4 cents per ounce for silver mined, not in all properties but in such new properties as are opened this year and which produce less than 40,000

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
ounces a month, and in such properties as were forced to close in 1938 because of the low price and which are reopened this year. It would be a comparatively small investment for the government, but it would be an excellent one, in view of the fact that it would put to work hundreds of young men and would reopen many properties. It would not affect any of the large mines. Last year there were produced in Canada 22,000,000 ounces of silver. I took the trouble to ascertain just what proportion of that production would be exempt from this excess price, and I found that 19,000,000 ounces would not be affected by it. I therefore ask the minister to consider this suggestion; to provide, in conjunction with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) this excess price for the product of newly operated properties. I am quite confident that the government will be making a very profitable investment, not only by saving the cost of the relief funds which are now paid to the unemployed, but in securing the sales tax on all materials which enter into the operation of these mining properties. The men who lease these properties-and most of them are leased-put their money into timbering, into . steel, into powder and equipment generally before the government provides a cent, and only if they get production would the government be called upon to pay anything over and above the world price for silver.
I hope the minister will give consideration to these and other suggestions which are intended simply for the purpose of relieving unemployment.

speechtext:
I feel that, from many points of view, the discussion in this house on the resolution to provide for relief assistance for the new fiscal year is the most important one which has arisen during the present session. So long as relief remains necessary, it will continue to be the centre of public attention, because the situation which gives rise to relief is one which must require the closest consideration by the members of the house and by the government of the day. Such observations as I shall make on this subject I wish to make without any partisan bias, without wishing to be critical of any government-whether past or present, whether federal or provincial- but rather in a spirit of helpfulness; for I heartily agree with that statement which is so frequently made, that only by united effort and concentrated study can Canada hope to eliminate the causes underlying the need for relief throughout the provinces.
In introducing this measure to the house on March 15, the Minister of Labour (Mr. 71492-180	*
Rogers) very properly outlined in a statistical manner the facts which stand behind the problem of relief administration. He showed the extent of the problem, translated into numbers of people who are existing as a result of the relief given to them by public authorities; he showed the main divisions of the problem of relief, and those main divisions indicate the causes for relief and suggest the general means which must be adopted if we are going to try to correct the present situation.
The minister showed that, in January of this year, of a total of 978,000 persons receiving relief to which the dominion contributes, about 32 per cent were on agricultural aid; that is to say, this percentage of those receiving aid are farmers and their dependents who, by reason of crop conditions, must have assistance. I would leave it to those more familiar with the farming industry than I am to suggest any solutions in the case of the problem of agriculture aid. During the last several years, as we all are only too well aware, crop conditions in the prairie provinces may be summed up as a series of disasters-drought, rust, grasshoppers and so forth. Even though those of us living in the parts of Canada which are not essentially agricultural have had our own problems to contend with, and still have to face all the consequences of continuing unemployment, I think we are all aware of what our fellow citizens on the prairies have had to go through, or of the uncertainties which large numbers of farmers still face, and are not unsympathetic to those measures of rehabilitation and assistance for the western farmer with which we are called upon from time to time to deal. We all hope that the time is not far distant when nature may once more deal kindly with the western farmer and when he may once again begin to receive a fair return for his labour and investment. Until that day comes, however, I for one shall always support any measure proposed which appears to offer any degree of advantage to the farmers who are afflicted.
In turning next to that phase' of the problem of relief which arises out of unemployment, I feel that I am on much more familiar ground than were I to undertake any discussion of the question of farm distress. Those of us who have worked for wages in any part of Canada during the past thirty-five years or so, know that unemployment is not a new problem, that there always have been persons willing and anxious to work who could not secure jobs no matter how much they needed them and no matter how painstaking they were in their search for employment. If any confirmation of such a statement is required,

2856	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
the statistics on the subject will provide abundant proof of the truth of this assertion. I would be the last to suggest, however, that because we have always had unemployment we should always have it. Surely a better arrangement of our economic system can be imagined than one that requires a percentage of our willing workers to rust away in idleness -at all times. Further, during the past ten years we have been the witnesses of a volume of unemployment which in earlier days, in pre-war days for example, we would have held to be unthinkable. I would not be the one to suggest that something has gone permanently wrong with our economic machine, and that, because before the war, we always had some unemployed we must now complaisantly take it for granted that at all times we shall have a much larger army of unemployed in our midst. With heavier unemployment it becomes all the more important for governments to seek out the means of correcting the situation and to endeavour to reduce to a minimum the number of our citizens who are without jobs.
More than once the present Minister of Labour has insisted that no one cure for unemployment which has been proposed up to this time, either in Canada or abroad, can be applied overnight to correct the whole situation. As an old trade union member I can claim to be one of those who, through trade union interest, have been required to give a great deal of thought and study to means of eliminating unemployment, and as a trade unionist I must admit that, even though trade unions represent the people who are actually affected by unemployment, the trade union movement in this and other countries has not yet been able to bring forward a formula which it could be claimed would cure unemployment if immediately and fully put into effect. Trade unions here and elsewhere have advanced many admirable suggestions, many of which have been given effect to with beneficial results. But I take it as deeply significant that the thoughtful consideration given by the workers' representatives to problems of unemployment has not resulted in the adoption by the trade union movement anywhere of a platform which it could be claimed would "mop up" unemployment in very brief order. The constant advocating of unemployment insurance by the trade unionists is an admission that unemployment to some extent seems inevitable. Incidentally, on this subject of unemployment insurance I wish once again to express hearty support of the efforts of the government to secure agreement on the part of the provinces to a measure of this sort in

Canada. One can only add the hope that the agreement of the provinces to the dominion proposal may not be delayed indefinitely.
We hear different cures for unemployment suggested from time to time, single remedies which only need to be applied for a brief interval to put everybody back to work at good wages. Obviously all of these cures cannot ibe right because frequently one contradicts the others. After experiments which we have seen in other countries one is entitled to feel that while many of these cures may have some merit, and if cautiously applied would ibe of some assistance, no one of them possesses all the strong points which its advocates claim. We know that a survey of unemployment made in the United States late in 1937 showed almost six million persons in that country then unemployed, apart from those on relief works, yet this followed after the most gigantic measures taken by any country in modern times to put people back at work. We cannot say that the United States experiment has failed; for presumably the situation there would be still worse were it not for the new deal, but we can conclude that, in spite of the tremendous expenditures of the government of that republic, large , numbers of people are still without work. Conditions being so closely similar in many respects in Canada and the United States, it is not difficult to see what the government here has been up against during these depression years. On the one hand we do not have the wealth to expend that the United States has, and on the other we could probably not hope for much greater success than our United States friends even if we had comparable sums to pay out for a new deal.
Early in the life of the present government a trade agreement with the United States was concluded, and that agreement has meant a great deal of extra business for Canadians. During the present session we have spent much time in debating a second agreement with the United States, which should still further extend our trade with our neighbour, and also assist us indirectly by facilitating the expansion of trade between Great Britain and the United States. I am one who believes that, given anything like normal conditions throughout the world, a policy of reciprocal trade treaties with the leading trading nations would produce unbounded prosperity in Canada. But although such treaties are, under any circumstances, a business necessity for this country, the fact appears to Ibe that unsettled international affairs, paralyzing to business in many directions, seriously restrict the advantages which should flow from trade agreements; and while we should not overlook any opportunities

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
to conclude any further agreements of benefit to Canada, at least until international affairs are on a more harmonious basis we cannot rely upon trade treaties to provide the volume of employment in Canada which we require effectively to minimize unemployment.
Measures which have been put into effect by the present government to ease conditions of unemployment have undoubtedly had beneficial effects. The expansion of the winter farm employment plan in the western provinces, the extension of assistance towards housing construction, the assistance in the training of youth in industry, the assistance for the rehabilitation of middle-aged industrial workers, the loans for self-supporting municipal utilities, the home improvement plan-these measures have all been beneficial; and while of themselves contributing substantially to the volume of employment offered, they have indicated what may be done through prudent government assistance.
As a member of this house, however- and I think all hon. members, whether they admit it or not, must have come to the same view-I have been deeply impressed by the habit of the public of always looking to the dominion government for assistance and completely overlooking the constitutional importance of the provincial governments in our scheme of laws and administration. To a very large extent the measures which this government has sought to operate to relieve unemployment have depended upon the goodwill and cooperation of the provincial governments. It would perhaps be much better if the public would shift some of the pressure which is constantly placed upon the dominion and apply it to the several provincial legislatures, to see to it that full cooperation is given by them to the dominion for the common good of Canadians. One cannot sit in this house for a number of years without realizing that the dominion government is not all-powerful, that a great deal of power rests with the provinces. In times such as these it is not enough that the provinces shall do their best within their sphere and that the dominion shall do its best within its sphere; it is extremely important that the provinces and the dominion shall work together on this grave problem of unemployment.
Until the world outlook becomes more promising, until we can look to external trade to furnish a larger volume of employment here in Canada, we must expect to continue those measures to relieve unemployment to which I have already referred, and must expect to spend even an increased amount on public construction, forestry projects, road building and the like. It is not enough for 71492-180J
us constantly to dwell on what a great country we have, how magnificent are our distances and how boundless our resources. Admittedly our population is not large in relation to our area, but since there is no immediate prospect of our population increasing rapidly we must make the best of the population we have. We cannot do this in any better way than by utilizing idle labour to develop those boundless resources and to provide transportation and other facilities to the limit to bridge our great, distances.	'
I disagree definitely with those who speak of money spent during the depression in relieving unemployment as wasted, in the sense that we have nothing to show for the expenditures we have made. We have provided ourselves with a number of splendid public buildings, we have improved our roads appreciably-and this means a great deal in such sections of the country as northern Ontario, which had been overlooked in the matter of roads until recent times-we have made our public parks more attractive for tourists, thereby improving the country's facilities to earn money. In carrying out these works the money spent has not been wasted; not only have we visible results to show but we have maintained the morale of the workers engaged on these projects by giving them an opportunity to earn money. As far as public projects of this sort are concerned, we have not overbuilt and we have not overspent, and as long as I continue to be a member of this house I shall support any further votes for like projects, and shall advocate that they be, if anything, on an increased scale. To repeat: money devoted to such purposes is far from being wasted, and I do not feel that those who claim that such moneys are wasted have a real understanding of the problem of unemployment or an abiding sympathy with unemployed workers; they simply lack an understanding of the fact that a man who is unemployed as far as industry is concerned, if he is used on a necessary public project is a much better citizen, and that it pays to spend money when necessary for a purpose of that kind.
There is one further suggestion which I have to make at this time, and which I consider to be of some importance. I do not need to weary the house by presenting statistics to prove that at all times we must look to private industry to provide the largest volume of employment for Canadians. Our whole system of government and industry is built on that principle. If at times we find it necessary to supplement private endeavour by public expenditures it is only as
2858	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
a stop-gap, and not because we have lost faith permanently in private industry to provide work for our people. In times such as these, on account of curtailment of markets abroad and anxiety and nervousness on the part of those who constitute the management of private business, there is not the tendency that there ought to be to develop new lines which would offer new avenues of employment. There is no doubt that nature has blessed us with a variety of natural resources, but it is up to us to put these resources to account by employing labour in the production of the commodities which we need. Without advocating high tariffs, I might call attention to the fact that present tariffs afford a fairly high percentage of protection to Canadian industry and to new industry which may be set up in the future for the purpose of utilizing our raw materials.
We often hear complaint made even in this house of the large numbers of public officials that we have in Canada. I am not one who has voiced these criticisms; I feel that in the main there is good and sufficient reason for having the number of public officials that we have. I do, however, feel keenly that the work of these public officials is not always turned to the greatest possible advantage, and in one particular direction to *which I wish to refer I believe this to be abundantly true. In the dominion government service there are large numbers of officials and employees engaged in cataloguing our natural resources.:	The provinces
also do a good deal of effective work along this line. On the other hand, we have numerous officers with technical training, for instance, in the national research council, the Department of Mines, the Department of Agriculture and so on, who devote their lives to research into the uses which can be made of Canadian resources. To some extent the provinces, and many of the larger cities, are constantly on the hunt for new industries.
Through trade statistics we have knowledge of those materials which we import which, with present tariff protection, could be manufactured economically from Canadian resources. What I have to propose is this: that there be set up a permanent body-call it a committee or a commission or what you will-of competent officials who would confer with private industry and with the various dominion, provincial and even municipal officers, studying and experimenting with resources and seeking to establish new industries, in order to discover ways and means of setting up new businesses which would give work to Canadians. In my mind there is no doubt that in the past we have

been too much inclined to leave this field to private business. That may have been well enough when there was work available for nearly everybody, but now that conditions have changed and that we must go out looking for means of employment, I suggest that there is no better way to find it than by correlating existing information and applying it specifically to the task of devising new industries w'hich might hope to succeed in Canada.
I know of no dominion government bureau that is definitely charged with this responsibility, and I think there should be one. The expenditure involved would be a mere fraction of the benefit to Canada, of what it would mean to this government in taxation revenue from newr industries, and of what we would save by providing jobs for thousands of Canadians. As I see it, this is largely a matter of collecting the information and the results of studies now available, for which we are already paying, in order that this material might be put to use in a practical way to provide assistance for our citizens. As a practical proposition there should not be a large additional expenditure involved, and I submit in all seriousness that this suggestion is well w'orth carrying out. I commend it to parliament and to the government as one means of adding to the payrolls of the country while at the same time adding to the prosperity of the community. I cannot help feeling that such a bureau, to coordinate, information in regard to what new industries might be set up to make use of existing materials and human resources, is something with which we should go ahead without delay.
The other measures to relieve unemployment are all excellent in their way, but we must recognize the fact that they are only temporary. New industries would give a permanence to the employment of Canadians which cannot be secured through short-term measures. From time to time new industries spring up through the foresight of some individual. Let us as a parliament assist that process. Let us, by more specific attention to these matters, anticipate the future; and rather than wait for individuals to act without urging, let the government assemble the facts and give an impetus to industry. Such a move is bound to result in increased employment if our confidence in the resources of our people and our country is justified; and I feel that our confidence certainly is justified.
Mr. J. A. MARSH (Hamilton West); Mr. Speaker, the government of this country cannot have realized the extent of this problem of unemployment. Had they done so, more

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
constructive means would have been taken during the last few years and more adequate legislation would be before us now to deal with it. We have had the problem for years; it is not new. It is not a temporary problem, or one that is getting any less in my riding; on the contrary it is getting worse.
Since I have been in this house I have made several speeches on the unemployment problem and have listened to many other speeches on the same subject, some of them very good and some not so good. Every plan on earth has been brought to the attention of this government for consideration, yet I am afraid very little has been done to cope with this problem by means of legislation. I am not going to contribute any lengthy remarks to this debate. I am going to read into Hansard the relief figures for the city of Hamilton for the last three years, and I will let those figures speak for themselves. On March 1, 1937, the number on relief in Hamilton was 14,300. On March 1, 1938, that number had increased to 17,600, and on March 1, 1939, there were 19,700 on relief. On April 1 of this year, just two weeks ago, that figure had reached 20,148. The population of Hamilton is approximately 158,000.
Those figures are from the welfare commissioner of the city of Hamilton. As far as I am concerned they indicate the inability of this government to govern and to solve the chief problem of Canada to-day. That is all I have to say. I am not surprised that I have received 2,100 ballots from people who are concerned with the future of this country. These people are very much interested in the government of Canada; in sending me their ballots they have also written sincere and intelligent letters. I do not take those ballots as a criticism of myself as a back-bencher of the opposition, although if any criticism is directed to me I am quite willing and anxious to assume my share of responsibility. I take them as criticism of the government.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, all I desire to say is that personally I will welcome more ballots, more interest in public affairs on the part of people and an early election.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on both occasions when I have had the honour of speaking in this house I have dealt mainly with the subject of unemployment, because I consider it the paramount question in Canada to-day. In view of the fact that we have a large country with a very small population, a country rich in land and all kinds of natural resources, it is difficult for me to understand why this should be our most important question. Unemployment was
first prevalent in Europe, I understand, and an attempt was made to cure it by sending people to new countries, such as Canada, where land could be obtained easily and cheaply. Now we find ourselves faced with the situation that at one time we helped to solve.
The alleviation of distress caused by unemployment has been during the past nine years a stubborn and persistent problem in practically every country in the world. Following the world-wide economic disturbances of 1929 and 1930 employment has been affected by industrial changes to such an extent that the re-employment of idle workers has fallen far behind the recoveries which have taken place in business generally. The principle of recognizing large scale unemployment as a permanent condition is being accepted in many countries, but surely there are few Canadians willing to accept that principle as applicable to a young, vigorous and richly endowed country such as Canada.
During the last nine years this calamity has cost this [DOT] government alone something like 8315,000,000. That, sir, is a tremendous amount of money, but in spite of this expenditure there were still in this great country of ours nearly 214,000 heads of families and their dependents on relief, as of November 1 of last year. We might overlook that amount of $315,000,000 if this problem had been cleaned up, or even if the end were in sight, but that is not the case. So I say, Mr. Speaker, that any war, particularly an internal one, that has gone on for over nine years and that has cost about $850,000,000, including the money spent by the dominion, the provinces and the municipalities, without counting the greatest cost of all which is the cost to our youth and the general suffering and misery which those on relief are experiencing, no longer can be considered a temporary condition. It must be looked upon as a national calamity and must be dealt with from a national point of view.
There is work of all kinds to be done in this dominion right now, work of a kind that will make Canada a greater, better country, and at the same time build up our national income. Some of these works I have mentioned in this house previously, but I intend to	repeat them	now.	First, there	is thetourist industry,	which	is the third	largestin	Canada. Let	us complete a good, wide,hard-surface highway from one end of the dominion to the other, with connecting links to	our national	parks	and to the	United
States. Let us eliminate all dangerous railway
2860	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
crossings, either by means of subways or by overhead crossings, in order to provide a complete safeguard against train accidents. In the unprotected sections we might plant the proper kind of trees, which would not only beautify the highway but act as a permanent snow fence and enable the road to be kept open longer for tourist business.
Then there is the important work of reforestation. In my own riding of Springfield, where millions of cords of pulp and cordwood and thousands of railway ties, as well as millions of feet of lumber, have been cut during the past thirty or forty years, the question of reforestation is now one of vital con. cern. At Pine Falls in my riding we have the only paper mill in the three prairie provinces. Here is one way of placing thousands of our young people at work over a long period of years, doing something to-day w'hich will benefit the generation of to-morrow; in other words, building up the country.-
I now come to the subject of water conservation. Here also, sir, is where many thousands of men could be put to work to do something of great national value. I give the government much credit for what it has already done in this regard under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, but I would suggest that it should be extended many times over and that it should include the constituency of Springfield.
Turning now to the subject of the supply of electricity in rural homes, I believe that through cooperation with the provinces the government should try to extend this convenience to nearly all farm homes. I mentioned last year that one of the reasons why so many of our young rural people are found unemployed in our cities is that they have not even a few of the simple conveniences, such as electric light and power, which city people enjoy. I believe the extension of power and light to the rural areas, particularly in the west, would do a great deal to curb the flow of our young people to the cities.
With respect to mining development I would say that here is a great industry that could be developed or expanded many times over. It is about the only industry I know of which in late years has really done something worth . while to help the labour situation. The mining roads have done a great deal towards helping, but the government should go farther in that direction. If we had better transportation facilities, particularly in our great north country, this would open up more mines and give still greater opportunities to thousands of our own people to get gainful work in that industry. I note the minister has in his
(Mr. Turner ]
estimates this year a substantial amount to be spent on mining roads, and I hope there is still more to come.
I turn now to the subject of sugar-beet and canning factories. Here also we have an opportunity to put many men to work. As I have said before in the house, the Manitoba government has already gone on record as backing the bonds of a sugar-beet factory to the extent of $600,000. I understand a sugar-beet factory will employ about fifty permanent employees, about 250 temporary employees, and also a great many more during the tending operations and at harvest time. This is something the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) might well consider. An extension along this line would help the farmers, who could stand a little extra cash at this time.
I now turn to youth training. May I heartily congratulate the Minister of Labour upon what he has already done in this direction, and more particularly upon what he has outlined in the companion resolution introduced at the same time as the one we are now discussing. I notice he has increased the expenditure for youth training to $4,500,000. I sincerely hope the government will see fit to establish a youth training school in my constituency.
I have tried to outline suggestions which I believe would add to the wealth of the country, and at the same time provide employment. May I repeat those suggestions:
1.	Trans-Canada highway, and connecting links with our national -parks, and the United States.
2.	Reforestation.
3.	Water conservation.
4.	Extension of electric light and power to rural areas.
5.	Mining development and mining roads.
6.	Sugar-beet and canning factories.
7.	Youth training.
Very few hon. members have risen in their places and offered solutions to this great problem. I believe, however, the one offered by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), which in short is to the effect that Canada can increase her money supply to an amount of four billion dollars without going into debt, and apply it towards relieving unemployment in works such as I have already mentioned, and others I could have indicated, should receive the serious attention of the government. May I add I had a letter from Mr. Clifford Barclay, of Tyndall, Manitoba, who sat for nine years in the Manitoba legislature, and from others, sharing this view. I believe the suggestion is at least worthy of close investigation.

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
There has always been seasonal unemployment in varying degrees in Canada. It is agreed that provision should be made for the care of the workers of the country during periods of enforced idleness. This government has announced its intention to put into effect a plan of "unemployment insurance" as soon as constitutional barriers have been eliminated. Briefly speaking, I should like to see the government use all the power at its command to bring all the natural resources and wealth and, last but not least, all the brain power available into play in a concerted effort tcf solve this problem.
May I repeat that an enormous amount of money has been spent by governments on this serious matter, and I believe, as I said at the outset, that the question is a national one and should be treated from that point of view. Therefore I would urge upon the government that in fairness to our hard working Minister of Labour it should take over all unemployment and relief, and set up a new department or board responsible directly to him to concentrate on this one problem. This question is too large to be involved with any other department. If it could be straightened out, I believe all our unrest and the differences existing among the various provinces would pass away. I do ask that this serious matter receive the attention it deserves.
The reasoning that the government must prepare to care permanently for large numbers of unemployed cannot be accepted by the average Canadian, and there is an evergrowing belief throughout the country that the final solution lies in the expansion of private industry, with the government assisting within its powers by maintaining conditions which will ensure that expansion. Let me add that if private industry or the so-called capitalistic system is to continue in this country under a high protection, then it is certainly up to these protected interests to carry their fair load of the problem of unemployment. That is only common sense.
I note that the resolution calls for alleviation of unemployment and agricultural distress. I believe this would be as good a time as any, because I do not speak very often in the house, to say that in my judgment the setting of the initial price of wheat at sixty cents, or very close to that amount, is adopting the principle of contraction, and I am bitterly opposed to it. It will mean that the railways will be the first to be affected, through lack of business, and will mean the laying off of employees all along both lines, because at that very low price the farmers will not deliver any more wheat than they have to.
Every industry, particularly machinery, and so forth, will similarly suffer. At this time the government should adopt the principle of expansion, and keep the price at eighty cents or higher, if it wants to lessen unemployment, and prevent our municipalities from going into bankruptcy. Does anyone suggest we can cut the purchasing power of our farmers by twenty-five per cent without seriously affecting unemployment?
In conclusion, to the youth of the country I would say that Canada is still a land of opportunity, whose natural resources per capita are perhaps the greatest of any land. Youth should not be willing to accept the dark picture which is too often painted for them by those who should know better. Recent years have been difficult, but as Canadians, whether young or old, we must regain the old-time pioneering spirit which conquered greater difficulties than those which confront us to-day. .

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to dwell at length on this subject, although to-day, as in 1930, and also in 1935, it is perhaps the most important question with which parliament has to deal. The observations I shall make will certainly not be in criticism of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) or the government. Like most hon. members who have spoken I wish to say that no doubt the minister and the government are doing their very best in a difficult situation.
Nevertheless I feel something more should and can be done. From my experience it is my view that most countries will settle their troubles by paying more attention to the rural districts and the people who populate those districts. The statement that mother earth will provide a living for any man, woman or family who will diligently cultivate the soil, is as true to-day as it ever was.
Our thoughts go back to the land to see if to a certain extent we cannot solve the problems which confront us. I would remind the house once more that through the farm placement scheme, which I am willing to admit was adopted by the former government, at the suggestion of the provincial deputy minister of labour in Winnipeg, and which, with certain added provisions, was carried on by the present government, we were able to close the relief camps of this country. That was done by putting the single unemployed out among the farmers. In doing that, I believe I am safe in saying that we cut by two-thirds the cost of main-
2862	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
taining those single unemployed. If I remember rightly, the minister gave the cost of maintaining the relief camps during the last year they were in operation as 811,000,000. The following year we had the farm placement plan, and we were able to close up the relief camps. It cost the taxpayers of the dominion only something over $3,000,000 to place thousands of men on farms.
We all know that when the spring opens up, thousands of men who are now idle in the cities will have an opportunity to get out and help the farmers put in their seed. We all know that they march to the harvest fields even though they have been unemployed during the summer months. They look forward to the time when they can get out to help to garner the crops. I can remember quite well many years ago when we used to have what we termed in western Canada the eastern invasion. We welcomed that invasion. At that time western Canada was able to absorb 30,000 to 35,000 young men and some women from eastern Canada. Of course, conditions have changed and harvest excursions to western Canada are now a thing of the past.
In reply to a question asked the other day the minister stated that 1,500 single unemployed had been taken from Ottawa last summer and placed on farms. I believe that a possible solution of our unemployment problem is the settling of people on the land. The employment commission recommended that a more extensive farm settlement scheme be evolved. At the present time we have a back-to-the-land scheme which is participated in by federal, provincial and municipal governments. I do not need to tell hon. members or to remind the minister-in fact he has reminded us of this fact-that this scheme has been only a partial success. I understand it has been discontinued in some of the provinces.
1 received a letter only this morning from a young married man with a family of six or seven small children. He was placed on a farm under this back-to-the-land scheme, but after three or perhaps more years he found the going so hard that he had to move back to the city of Winnipeg. This man had hard luck because he lost his horses on account of the sleeping sickness which was so prevalent in western Canada. He was on his farm during a period of poor crops and low prices. It was a most inopportune time for him to go on the farm. He drifted back to the city after trying to get work as a carpenter- 
and he is a good one. He is now making an effort to be reestablished on the land, and I should like to quote the following from his letter:
You know the difficult position we were in out there. We sold out last fall because we had lost so many horses and then on top of that the poor crops. We could not get any assistance from them-
I believe he is speaking about the rehabilitation committee in Winnipeg.
[DOT]-so they told me. I had hopes of being able *to get enough work at the building trade but that is pretty slack so I have put in an application for resettlement but was told that the dominion government was thumbs down on any resettlement under the rural rehabilitation scheme.
I draw that to the attention of the minister because it seems to me that we are standing in our own light. I know this man and I know his wife who was born in my own district. They are hard working, industrious people and they should have another chance. Why allow this man to drift into the city and possibly displace somebody else who is not capable of taking up habitation on the land?

speechtext: Why should this government make an exception?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: If I may be allowed to continue with my remarks-

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: The hon. member cannot answer that.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Yes, I can answer it. There should not be any exception; they should all have consideration. I say to the government, I say to the minister and I say to this house: It is time that we adopted some intelligent scheme for keeping our people on the farms and for resettling our land. Some years ago -I believe it was during the first session of this parliament-I directed the attention of the house to a resettlement scheme. I believed that such a scheme would keep our people on the land instead of having them drift into the cities. I am not going to go into that again, except to say that the federal government should at least take a lead in regard to this matter. I am not arguing that they should undertake any expenditures or work out an intricate policy without the aid and advice of the provincial governments, but I do think they should show a lead. I suggest to the government that they should take up this matter with the provincial governments and the municipalities.
The first thing they should do is to try to make conditions on the farm so attractive that the young people will want to stay there.

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
That condition does not exist at the present time. If we are going to keep our young people on the land, we shall have to make conditions such as to make them want to stay there. My proposition to the government at that time was that by working through the municipalities, which were in the best position to know conditions in the immediate district, and through the provincial governments, they could find out how many young men were willing to stay on the old homesteads and carry on the business of farming.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Before six o'clock I was pointing out a method whereby the government might make conditions better for those who till the soil. I used the word "attractive" -make farming more attractive. One hon. member suggested to me that in order to make it more attractive perhaps we should have a radio on the plough and a telephone at each headland, but really that is not what I had in mind. Perhaps it would have been better if. instead of using the word "attractive," I had used the word "secure."
The plan which I mapped out in a previous session is, in a few words, as follows. I believe the dominion government should take the initiative in this work and say to any province that wishes to cooperate with them, "We are willing to offer financial assistance to your government if you will join with us in a scheme to stop the drift of our farm population to the cities." It is, I think, for the dominion government to accept the financial responsibility. They should be prepared to loan money to the provinces, which would take the matter up with each municipality. The officials of the municipality, who are right on the ground floor, knowing their people in every part of the district, are in a position to take an inventory of not only lands available for resettlement but lands which the present holders are trying to farm but a part of which they would be extremely glad to sell to anyone who had the cash. The provincial government could take note of these inventories, communicate with the dominion, and say, "We have plenty of land in various districts, and we have many young men who would like nothing better than to set up a home either on part of their fathers' lands or elsewhere." Then the three organizations working together could purchase this land,
title being taken, of course, in the name ol the crown. It would be hard to get a better investment. The land could be resold to a farmer's son or some other young man who wished to farm.
I believe the effect would be to keep many of the older people on the land because they would have less responsibility; they perhaps would be in a position to pay off the mortgages on their farms. At the same time the young men would be satisfied to settle on these farms, because they would have good land, the price would not be exorbitant, and the rate of interest would be low; by this means thousands of young people would be retained in the rural districts. If you keep the young men on the soil it naturally follows [DOT] that you will keep the young women there also. I shall not go into this scheme in detail at this time. I did so on a previous occasion. I submitted it to the employment commission which operated last year, and anyone who cares to turn up their files will find it in detail there.
The problem of keeping people on the soil is one which is bothering the wits of every nation. I picked up a paper to-day and cut out this clipping with regard to Ireland, "Youth wanted on farm":
Ireland is trying to solve the problem of where to place its youth. Because of the slump in agriculture farmers are sending their children to Dublin and other cities to take up professions, all of which are crowded. Not only the poor but the middle classes as well have difficulty in finding employment for their young. Government leaders are being criticized for not making farming more lucrative and thus more attractive to young people.
At Portage la Prairie, my own city, there was held this winter a rural class under the youth training scheme. It was my privilege to visit that class before coming to Ottawa. At that time-I believe that the class has since been disbanded for this year-there were over fifty in attendance, with able instructors. I was informed that the class was most enthusiastic. I knew personally most of the boys; nearly all of them came from farm homes; I believe that every one of them would like nothing better than to get on to a farm and start a home for himself if he could possibly make his farm pay, and it should be our job to see that these boys do make it pay. I do not want the house to take that literally. I know it is not the duty of a government to see that everyone makes a profit; people must exercise their own brains, ability and knowledge. But there is something lacking in agriculture at the present time because men with brains, ability and knowledge are falling by the wayside every'



Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
year. Speaking as a farmer, I believe that something can be done by this government along the lines I have suggested to keep these men on the farms rather than have them drift into the cities to displace working men there.
In conclusion, I should like to say that the government has a hard task, one which will need all its ingenuity and ability. I appeal to all hon. members in this matter: I believe that the government should have the cooperation of every member-

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Unemployment is one of Canada's most urgent problems. It has been a serious problem in this country for man}' years, because unemployment means poverty and distress; unemployment means want and misery walking throughout the land. I am reminded that a Conservative government promised before the election of 1930 that they would solve the problem of unemployment. They failed to do so. The Liberal government did not promise to solve the problem of unemployment, but they promised to abolish poverty, which is the result of unemployment, and in this connection I refer to the statement made on the night of the election by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). He said:
In the new era which dawns to-day, the struggle for the rights of the people will, in the realm of economic liberty and security, be carried on as never before. Poverty and adversity, want and misery, are the enemies which Liberalism will seek to banish from our land. They have lain in wait at the gate of every Canadian home during the past five years, and their menacing mien has served to destroy the souls, as well as the minds and bodies, of an everincreasing number of men, women and children in our land.
We take up at once, as our supreme task, the endeavour to end poverty in the midst of plenty, starvation and unnecessary suffering in a land of abundance, suffering and distress in a country more blessed by providence than any other on the face of the globe, and to gain for individual lives, and for the nation as a whole, that "health and peace and sweet content" which is the rightful heritage of all.
If the government had carried out that promise instead of searching for means of providing employment; if they had fulfilled their promise to abolish poverty due to unemployment resulting from technical develop-

ments in the past, we would commend them. Unemployment has resulted from technical developments and is a consequence of industry having taken advantage of the work of scientists and inventors to displace man, to substitute the machine for man, to substitute solar energy for human energy-and, believe me, they have done a good job of it. The problem is one, not of providing work for people, but of getting rid of the poverty which has resulted from unemployment, many people believe that only through work can a man live, when as a matter of fact machinery power has displaced man power.
I will now indicate the impossibility under the present relief rates of abolishing poverty in this land. The other day a delegation of the unemployed visited me in my office and I asked them a few questions. I asked them whether the position of the relief recipient, of the unemployed, was any better to-day under the Liberal government than under the Conservative, and they said, "No." I said to them, "What do you fellows want anyway? What is it you are after?" They replied, "We want the right to secure a living in this country, a living which we feel can be produced from the abundance of our natural resources. We want a home. We want the right to marry. We want to know where we shall sleep at night and where we are going to eat. We want to live like other human beings." I asked, "Where are you sleeping now?" They answered, "We don't know; we have nowhere to sleep." I asked, "Where are you eating?" They answered, "We are eating in soup-kitchens"-they were transient unemployed. They said there were soup-kitchens in various parts of the country. I asked them where they were eating in Ottawa, and they said they got meals for two or three days and a bed ticket, and then were told to move on. The federal government will not assume the responsibility; the municipalities will not assume it, and the provincial governments refuse to take it. And so these men have to move back and forth across the country. They are no better off than when they were in the camps initiated by the previous Conservative government.
Last year I asked the minister to give the relief rates paid in Canada. These are the figures:

That is the per capita relief paid for food, clothing and shelter for one month. The relief rate is no different now from the relief rate paid under the Conservative government. The condition of these people is no better than it has ever been.
Let me now cite some figures given by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). The usual charge for food and other things required daily are from S12 to S15 a month. That does not cover overhead, wages of guards, cost of buildings and so on; it covers only the maintenance of prisoners. In other words, in answer to a question I directed to the Minister of Justice as to how much it costs to keep a prisoner in gaol he said that it cost this government from $12 to $15 a month, just for maintenance, not including wages of guards, overhead, cost of buildings and so on. Let us see how that works out.
A Canadian on relief in Prince Edward Island receives, from the sums provided by the municipal, provincial and federal governments, $2.24 a month for material aid-that is, for fuel, food, clothing and shelter. For the year a Canadian on relief in that province would receive, for material aid, $24.88. A family of six good Canadians would receive in that province for material aid, contributed to by the three governments, the sum of $149.58. It costs the federal government alone from $144 to $180 a year to keep a criminal in the penitentiary-and he gets little enough. In other words, for six prisoners in the penitentiary the government has to put up from $864 to $1,080, just six or eight times as much as it costs to keep six persons on relief in Prince Edward Island.

speechtext:
My hon. friend is giving,
of course, the per capita cost of relief in the various provinces. He is not giving the relief scales. For example, a family with five children would receive at the per capita cost over the dominion, which the hon. member stated to be $6.43, a total of $45 a month. I mention that, so that there will be no misunderstanding of the figures my hon. friend gives.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
The average varies
from province to province and from municipality to municipality. In fact, in the suburbs of a town a different rate is paid, and even in the same town the rates vary.
Here is the situation that does obtain in Prince Edward Island, for example. It costs the government from eight to ten times as much to keep a prisoner in gaol as to keep a man on relief. In Nova Scotia a Canadian on relief receives $4.49 a month for material aid-fuel, food, clothing and shelter-or $53.88 71492-1814
for one year, from the three governments. A family of six would receive S323.28. In Manitoba a good Canadian citizen on relief receives $6.50 a month or, for one year, $78, from the three governments who share the cost of relief. A family of six would receive $468 for the year. It costs this government alone from S864 to $1,080 to keep six criminals in the penitentiary-pickpockets, bank robbers, and so on. In Alberta, a good, law-abiding Canadian citizen receives $6.78 a month for material aid, or $81.36 for one year, and a family of six would receive $488.16; yet it costs the federal government from $864 to $1,080 to keep six criminals in the penitentiary. In British Columbia a citizen on relief receives $7.67 a month, or $92.04 a year for material aid. A family of six receives from the three governments $552.24 a year for material aid; yet to keep six bank robbers in gaol costs the government $864 to $1,080 a year just for the daily requirements. There would be a good deal more space between the vests and the desks of hon. members if they had to live on that relief rate.
The problem is not to find work for these people; it is to abolish poverty. That is what the Liberal party said they were going to do, but they have not fulfilled that promise. If it were a matter of lack of goods, of lack of production; if it is not realized that we are in an age of plenty, then I suggest to the minister that he read the statistics showing the production of Canada and how 234,000 men in Canada can produce $1,400,000,000 worth of commodities. Put the 450,000 people who are prepared to go to work in Canada to-day to work and you will produce billions of dollars' worth of new wealth. No, it is not a question of producing wealth; we cannot get rid of what we have, of what we are producing to-day. The government say, Let us restore confidence. You may buy with confidence,-but you cannot pay for goods with confidence. You must pay for them with money. People have to have increased purchasing power before they can buy anything.
I refer to a statement made by the Prime Minister in regard to unemployment and to what this government has done towards solving the problem of unemployment. He said, as reported at page 64 of Hansard'. ,
I am surprised that members of this parliament, I care not to what particular party they may belong, should seek continually to persuade the people of this country that this parliament has not been doing what it should for unemployment, or that the unemployment question is what it is to-day because of some lack of effort here at Ottawa. Hon. members of this house are responsible for what is done with the public funds of this country raised by federal taxation. Instead of belittling what has been
2866	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
done, why do they not point out to the people of Canada what has been done by the parliament to which they belong^ and by the government at Ottawa, since this government operates by virtue of the power given it by this parliament? Why do they not take upon themselves to show the people that session after session this government has passed measures to assist in the relief of unemployment; that year in year out it has been giving more and more and more in the way of public funds to the provinces to help them in working out their share of the solution?
Well, what is the result? Last year the premier of Ontario said that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) had offered no effective solution of the question of unemployment, and he said that the speech made by the Minister of Labour was a headache. Well, after he reads the one the minister made this year he had better reach for his aspirin tablets, because he is going to have another headache.
The other day the mayors had a conference in Ottawa and went away dissatisfied. They are carrying on radio broadcasts at the moment asking the federal government to assume complete responsibility for the cost of financing relief. I listened to Mayor Houde of Montreal last night declaring that it cost him 4-61 per cent to capitalize relief costs in that city. The governments, that is, municipal, provincial and federal, who contribute to relief, have spent somewhere in the neighbourhood of $900,000,000 on relief since the depression started. I believe that it is somewhere in the neighbourhood of $480,000,000 that the provinces have borrowed in order to maintain relief. The federal government say that last year they spent $17,000,000 on relief. Now they are paying as much in interest to the bondholders as they are paying out on relief- possibly a good deal more. I wish the minister would get the figures and check up, find out how much the bondholders are making in interest on the money that has been spent for relief purposes. He will find that they are making a considerable amount of money, capitalizing on the poverty in this country.
As I say, the Conservative party failed to solve unemployment, and the Liberal party cannot find work for the unemployed. The government of the United States have spent billions of dollars trying to put the people to work, through PWA projects, WPA projects and CCC projects, but they still have a tremendous number of unemployed. I am absolutely in accord with the attempt made by the government of the United States to solve the problem of unemployment. By doing so they minimize the effect of poverty. I know that those who were single unemployed transients in the United States were 
put in CCC camps and given a dollar a day; the WPA workers are busy throughout the country building ' highways and parks; the PWA workers are busy throughout the land building schools and other government buildings, and they are receiving wages and salaries which help to maintain the economic system of the United States to some extent through the expenditure of the money they receive. But the United States government has been unable to cure unemployment. I agree with anyone who says that unemployment is here to stay; millions now living will never work again. We have to face that. But why? Because they have been displaced by the machine, must they live in abject poverty? That is the question I direct to the minister now.

speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman a solution to offer?

speechtext:

Mr. HANSON; How is that to come about?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I will tell hon. members how it is coming about. We have told them many times before, but I will go over it again.
Mr. HANSELL; When the Liberal party is defunct is when it will come about.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
This is another statement made by the Prime Minister:
Look at the financial statements of Britain to-day; look at the financial statements of the United States to-day, and see what proportion of the national income is going into war armaments or munitions and into the training of men for war. That has had another effect. It has had this effect. It has thrown capital out of productive industries and put it into unproductive industries, with the result that there is much less capital left to invest in anything of a productive character.
But it has had an even worse effect than that. It has helped to prevent the investment of capital altogether. It has had a paralyzing effect upon the investment of capital. That is the position, above everything else, of this country and of some other countries to-day. Men will not put out their money to invest in the different industries. They are withdrawing their capital from industry. Ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), who is sitting here to-night, how much of the investment of capital to-day is going into government securities at a low rate of interest in comparison with what took place in former years. It has deprived manufacturing industry and our primary industries, and the like, of the capital they need.
I am surprised that he should make that last statement that it has deprived manufacturing industry and our primary industries

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
of. the capital they need, when he had promised time and time again to issue money and credit in terms of public need. He continues:
Why is that? Fear is paralyzing people with regard to their savings, and they are not investing them for productive purposes.
There is nothing at all mysterious about that. What are people to invest their money in to-day with any assurance that they will be able to sell the goods? If the minister tvould talk to these men who have money to invest he would find them asking him what assurance they would have that they could sell the goods that they invested their money to produce. If someone were to build houses, or build apartments, because they had money to do it with, what assurance have they that they can sell them or rent them, with the relief rates, such as they are, being paid to the unemployed?
Assume that I had 810,000,000-just say I had-I see myself in a difficult position. Would I put my 810,000,000 into the production of coal in Alberta? I know there is plenty of coal there and I know there are many people cold in Alberta, also in Quebec and in Ontario, and all through Canada. People want more coal, but I am not going to put my money into the production of more coal because I know the people have not the money to buy it.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Put it into oil.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
It does not matter
what I put it into. If I want to manufacture radios, what is the position? I find that the factories are working part-time, that they are unable to sell the radios they are producing to-day unless they take fifty cents down and fifty cents the next time they catch you. If I want to manufacture automobiles I find the same thing. They cannot sell the automobiles they are producing to-day, and they are away below their productive capacity, as all industries are. They are not turning out all the goods they could produce. Why? Because they cannot sell what they have produced already; so they say, "What is the use of pi'oducing more when we cannot sell that which we have already produced?" Yet some hon. member rises in his place and asks me the question.
How is this problem to be solved? Why, millions of dollars worth of goods are sold every day on the instalment plan, and then some shark loan company comes along and says, "Here, we will save you from the sheriff. You are unable to meet your payments, so we will come to your rescue." People pay from twelve to twenty per cent more for every bit of merchandise they buy on the instalment plan; I think the average is about
twelve per cent, and then along comes the shark loan company and lends money at 24-8 per cent to make the payments due and save the goods from seizure. Yet the hon. member asks me, " What must we do to solve the problem?" My answer is: Give the people purchasing money so that they can buy the goods.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Is this socialism or fascism?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I cannot understand what the hon. member is saying. I notice I have only six minutes left, and I want to refer to a -book called National Economy and the Banking System of the United States, an-exposition of the principles of modem monetary science in their relation to the national economy and the banking system of the United States, by Robert L. Owen. At page 60 I find this:
The lack of stable, permanent employment compels labourers to demand higher prices for their labour when their employment is for comparatively short periods of time. This accounts for the complaint often lodged against labour when the labour unions fix wages at a price deemed too high. Such arbitrary high figures have a necessary tendency to prevent the building of houses for the shelter of labour.
The national policy of government should be directed to stabilizing employment. Stability of employment depends upon stability in the medium of exchange. There must be an adequate supply of money, neither too little nor too much, and only the government with its financial power and legal authority can accomplish this end.
By brain or by brawn, practically all of the people of the United States labour and are producers and consumers. A man of wealth directs the employment of his wealth, but as a consumer he draws no more in food or clothing than millions who are not wealthy. The accumulated wealth is distributed by law as the men of wealth die.
It is a grave fallacy to believe that scarcity is unavoidable or that abundance for all is unattainable because scarcity afflicts millions of people in a land of unlimited natural opportunities. Many men believe and have been taught to believe by suffering that scarcity is unavoidable; that there is a necessary limitation on the demand for labour; that many must of necessity go unemployed; that, therefore, the demand for employment should be distributed by a fewer number of working days and by a shorter number of working hours. A fewer number of working days and shorter hours will be justified when the American people shall have fully developed and fully employ the machines their inventive genius has developed, and the power produced through coal, petroleum water power, and electricity. This objective has not been achieved.
But until abundance for all is produced and full employment is provided through an adequate supply of the medium of exchange, the energy and intelligence of statesmen should be directed toward furnishing an adequate medium of exchange for the transfer of maximum products and services of the people to each other.
Labour leaders have had the artful appeal made to them that a rise in the index of the
2868	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
price level means a rise in the cost of living. This means this argument opposes a rise in the volume of the money required to create abundance and to create a larger volume of products. This argument has been shown oeretofore to be entirely fallacious beca'ise as the money supply rises employment and wages increase and of course the products increase in volume as labour increases in the number employed. When the volume of money and the volume of commodities rise together, as they do, the purchasing power of money remains unchanged and the average price of commodities remains unchanged as far as money is concerned.
In Loeb's "Chart of Plenty," which had its origin in the Department of Commerce and the labour of a number of experts, it has been demonstrated beyond the possibility of successful contradiction that with the existing machinery, technological processes, manpower, organization, increase of electrical energy, and our natural resources the people of the United States could easily produce $130,000,000,000 annually, if they were fully employed. This chart should be studied by patriotic men who desire our country to reach the highest standard of living for all of the people. It should be studied by those who desire to end human misery in the United States. It should be studied by those who desire equality of opportunity for the children who are daily born into the world. It should be studied by those who desire the farmers of the United States to have a fair reward for the hard labour they perform. It should appeal to those who have been disturbed by the growth of organizations based on discontent and which not only has caused a widespread demand for the protection of the weak and defenceless by the federal government, but has also caused the igrowth in this country of subversive organizations which regard democracy as incapable of -.giving all of the people sufficient food to live on.
There wras a great leader who proclaimed His purpose in entering the world that He came to bring life, and life more abundantly. He told His disciples the first means by which to accomplish it. As I remember it, He said, "Seek ye first the Kingdom of God and His righteousness and all these things shall be added unto you."
National prosperity and abundance cannot be founded on blind selfishness. "It must be founded upon the doctrine which declared, "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."
