In the following section I speak of the national consumers' dividend, which is omitted from this bill, and I would like to point out here another justification for the dividend- an economic justification. We are all familiar with what is known as the problem of technological unemployment. We knt>w_ that the purpose of labour-saving machinery is to save labour, is to displace men from industry, is to make them outcasts from industry. They are not wanted any more. A labour-displacing machine does fulfil its aim.
You cannot absorb those men expatriated from industry at the rate at which they are thrown out. It is perfectly true that you can absorb some of them. We can point to statistics from time to time and say that unemployment figures are down now, that there are new trades, new services, and that we are reabsorbing the unemployed. Nevertheless again it is a question of a rate, the rate at which they are being displaced from industry, which must be greater, thanks to modern invention and applied science, than the rate at which they can be reabsorbed into employment.
I also find this:
In the whole history of economics, I do not know of anything quite as audacious as the presentation of Douglas, not of a theory, but of a theorem, a statement that there is a " chronic and inherent deficiency of purchasing power. This is a challenge, and it is a challenge made only by an appeal to facts. The only question is, Is it true or not? It is irrelevant to argue about a theorem. The relevant thing to do is to test it experimentally.
We say that the A plus B theorem has been proved a priori, a posteriori, inductively and deductively. We say that you can get experimental proof of it every week in any factory, and if you set a cost expert to work, it will be discovered that during that week the cost of the products manufactured for the market will be greater than the sums distributed to the employees. The cost expert will prove that it is impossible for the individuals receiving income payments from a factory at the end of the week to buy back the products made in that factory during that week. This has been presented to orthodox economists in the world during the last twenty years, and a great many

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
of them remind me of the old lady who saw a giraffe for the first time and said, "I do not believe it." The orthodox economists have said, "I do not believe it," but they do something different from what the old lady did. The old lady did not go on to prove elaborately that such a creature as a giraffe could not possibly exist, which is what the orthodox economists have attempted.
Now, as I said before, a theorem has to do with rates, and rates are difficult for most of us to understand. Perhaps this illustration will clarify the matter. Let us consider the matter of births and deaths. Very well; every person who is born dies, and therefore the birth rate and the death rate are the same; therefore, population is stationary. We know of course that population is not stationary, that if the birth rate is faster than the death rate the population increases, and vice versa. If the mortality rate is faster than the birth rate, population declines.
In the United States they recognize that we have reached the age of abundance, and now it is simply a matter of distributing the goods that we are so capable of producing. The means by which these goods can be distributed is by having a proper medium of exchange in sufficient quantity to do the work.

speechtext: But the hon. member is not forgetting that on Friday night he said his policy would not solve the unemployment problem.

I did not say it would not solve the unemployment problem. I said it would not solve unemployment. I never said that the payment of a dividend would solve unemployment, but it will do this; It will take the people out of poverty, and it will give them the increased purchasing power which will turn the wheels of industry. Increased purchasing power put into industry will employ more men. The employment of more men means more wages and less unemployment. But it will never do away with all the unemployed, because the world over there is a surplus of labour which is idle and of goods which are unused.
Why, here is one illustration: Let us consider coal, for example. We have a certain market in Canada for coal. People in Russia want to ship coal to this market. People want to ship coal to this market from Wales. People want to ship coal to this market from the United States, and possibly from other countries. But we can supply all our needs in Canada. There are unemployed coal miners in Canada. There are unemployed coal miners in the United States. There are unemployed coal miners in Wales-I do not know whether there are any in Russia, or not.
The same thing would apply to machinery. Germany wants to ship farm machinery to
Canada. She wants to trade farm machinery for our wheat. But we have facilities in Canada to manufacture all the farm machinery we need, and more for purposes of export. The world has reached a period of plenty, but we have yet to learn how to distribute those goods. People to-day are suffering from the lack of goods that we are capable of producing in Canada. It is only a question of relating our monetary system to the facts. We must have our monetary system reflect our ability to produce and distribute the wealth of the country. It is not a difficult problem, but if you continue to borrow money for relief as you are doing to-day you will bankrupt the municipalities and bankrupt the provincial governments. You cannot bankrupt this government-they are only mentally bankrupt. That is the situation here.
If we would adjust our financial system and assume our responsibilities-adjust our money system-this problem would cease to exist. But what do we do? We try to borrow ourselves out of debt and tax our way to prosperity. It is no wonder the municipalities are asking the federal government to assume the responsibility for this problem. They are objecting, because the cost of relief is increasing taxes to such an extent that people will not build homes. We have reached a period of diminishing return so far as taxation is concerned, and still the government goes on, piling up debt, piling up taxes, and the unemployed continue to live at the rate of $6.43 a month for food, clothing and shelter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to make a few observations with regard to only one aspect of the unemployment problem, that relating to the non-resident or migrant unemployed, sometimes described as the single homeless men. I find it more difficult to discuss this subject than almost any other that could be mentioned. This is perhaps because I have had a direct and personal contact with this problem and have had some distressing and appalling revelations. I do not propose to indulge in any dispute as to statistics or to discuss at this stage any political or economic theories. I feel that certain statements should be made with regard to this problem because of its urgency and its present threatening aspect. I shall venture several suggestions which have been approved in various quarters throughout the dominion, which I believe to be practicable and which I believe could be adopted immediately without any constitutional amendment or without any serious dislocation of our economy.
I was impressed with a remark which was made by a friend of mine who has had a great deal of experience in dealing with single homeless men. He said that if to-morrow we could solve our unemployment problem, we would still be faced with the gigantic problem of the rehabilitation of our young men, made necessary because of conditions which have prevailed during recent years, because of their life of aimless wandering, because of their frustration, because of the instability and inactivity, and, he added, because of the cheap, greasy meals they have had to consume. He told me that it was appalling to consider all that was needed to be done again to deal
in a constructive way with the innumerable misfits which have been created as a result of policies pursued during recent years.
I do not wish to be unfairly critical or to berate the officials of the federal and provincial governments, but surely it must be as apparent to them as it is to me that the .present policy is much more costly and wasteful than would be a constructive national plan. Surely it must be apparent that in order to solve this problem we must have immediately the necessary leadership from the federal government. In no other way can we achieve an effective solution of the problem of the migrant or homeless single man. I hope the minister will discuss the dimensions of this problem frankly when either the resolution or the bill is in committee. At that time he may desire to correct me with regard to certain estimates of the problem which I intend to venture, but I should like to refer immediately to a statement made by the Canadian welfare council in their book entitled, The Problem of the Non-Resident and Migrant. They say this:
Some of the registration statistics, issued by the national employment commission, indicated that even at its lowest level, our non-resident and homeless men must have exceeded 50,000: doubtless the total has been as high as 100,000 at some times. Only those who are accepted as in receipt of aid as individuals in some one centre are registered and the general experience of our larger centres, (possibly a fair reflex of the movement through the smaller cities and towns) is that from a quarter to a third of the number aided at any time are non-resident. The more mobile elements in these groups are not likely to be stationary, unless in the depth of winter, for the one constant factor in local policy in many centres is to keep these men moving.
May I emphasize those last words where they say that the one constant factor in many centres is to keep these men moving. That has been my own experience, and it has been the experience recounted to me by scores of social service workers across Canada. For a moment I should like to touch upon my own personal experiences, which perhaps in many respects have been duplicated by other hon. members. I have had a direct personal contact with many young men in suburban communities. I refer to my own experiences because of the assertion which has often been made in this house that these men are not willing to work. My contact has been with young men in the age group between seventeen and twenty-two years who have demonstrated clearly their willingness to work. These young men when they have secured work have been accustomed to perform the most arduous manual labour. They, have done such work as cutting shingle bolts, cutting wood, packing rock, shovelling gravel, working in the canneries, and they have done
2872	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
occasional work in the bush. My experience has been that this work has been performed satisfactorily. But never hate they had an opportunity, of gaining permanent employment. To my personal knowledge on various occasions these young men have walked as many as eight or ten miles in order to look for work.
I have known some of them who in order to follow up some clue of possible work have actually had to be pried off the top of buses in an almost frozen condition after having attempted to get a ride. I have seen them attempting to ride the freight cars or hitchhiking in severe weather until their feet were in such terrible condition as to require medical treatment. There can be no doubt that this particular type of young man has a desire to secure work. They are the type of men who are transients in the making. On occasion I have discussed their problems with groups of these young men who have been engaged in a systematic endeavour to secure work. I have gone on their behalf to the employment service of Canada, but the officials of the service have said quite frankly that they had no answer to their problem. These young men may register if they so desire, but the officials could offer them no hope of employment, particularly when they were unskilled workers.
I have known them systematically to tramp the streets of Vancouver, calling at warehouses, departmental stores, making the rounds of the docks, going anywhere where there was any hope of work. They would do this morning after morning, making a careful canvass of all the opportunities of employment. Out of such a group only one or two would secure employment, and that employment would be of a most casual or temporary kind. There is one young man whom I know who secured work after the most strenuous efforts. A business man who had followed his efforts carefully finally secured temporary employment for him, but only at the rate of $6 a week. But he was severely handicapped because he did not have the necessary clothes, and there was no source to which he could turn to secure the clothes which his employers required him to wear when he was occasionally needed to meet the public.
I wonder if the officials here have any clear idea of how we are making transients? Some of these young men who are only seventeen or eighteen years of age started to ride the freights. They heard there might be work in the interior of British Columbia and they attempted to get to the different points. I followed the experiences of one group very closely. They boarded a freight in Vancouver, stopped off at Penticton and at various other

points in the interior, and finally came back through Kamloops and other points on that loop through the province. Most of the time they lived in jungle camps. They went from ranch to ranch in the interior of British Columbia seeking employment. I met this particular group of three or four young men later, and they had been living for three days on green apples and were completely discouraged. Nowhere could they find any work, and nowhere could they find any interest in their problem.
I desire to give full credit to those who are in charge of recreational centres or other training projects. When I applied on behalf of these men I was told that the quota was filled or that they were not eligible because their parents were not on relief. The majority of these young men to whom I refer are from homes where the parents were in receipt of very low incomes. They felt, and quite properly so, that they were a distinct burden on their parents. We are making transients by not giving proper attention to conditions confronting the young men of Canada. Again I emphasize the fact that they have demonstrated their willingness and eagerness to perform any kind of work at almost any wage. On behalf of this particular group I urge greater coordination between community efforts, the employment service and youth training projects. Otherwise these men are within a step of joining that greater group of wandering transients who are to-day without hope and without any elementary form of security.
My experiences also relate to the results of present policies. I visited Oakalla gaol in Vancouver just after 107 transients had been sentenced for what we call tin-canning, a technical breach of the law. It was generally recognized by the police officers, the police magistrates and the warden of Oakalla gaol that the men in the main were not criminals. They were sentenced for terms ranging from four to six months, and even at the time they were sentenced plans were in preparation in British Columbia for opening up ca,mps to care for these transients. W'hen I visited the gaol through the courtesy of the warden, I found a distressing situation. The warden made it clear that he was quite sympathetic, but after all he was running a gaol, not a hostel, and he had to enforce the regulations prescribed by the lieutenant-governor in council. The men on the other hand felt that they had a legitimate grievance. They had been given these long and severe sentences for what they thought was simply a technical breach of the law.

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
After all, as a result of their organized protest against almost intolerable conditions, within just about a week after they were sentenced all their comrades were permitted to go to camps specially arranged for in British Columbia. Finally they were released just before Christmas time by clemency exercised by the crown upon recommendation of the attorney general for British Columbia. But for three days pandemonium reigned in Oakalla gaol. The men, because of their grievances arising from scanty breakfasts and from overcrowding- two men were placed in cells intended for only one occupant-attempted to protest within the gaol and completely disorganized the prison routine. They were pounding their cots on the concrete floor, pounding their boots on the floor, rattling across the bars, and they refused to take their bedding back into the cells. Some were punished. Some were given solitary confinement. Some lost their shoes temporarily. All had their privileges curtailed. The whole thing was stopped immediately we could bring them assurance that the outside world had not forgotten them and their legitimate grievance. Surely imprisonment is not an answer to this problem. Imprisonment accentuates rather than ameliorates the problems of the single homeless man. One hundred and seven men in gaol may not seem important, but hundreds of others have been sentenced in Vancouver in the past year. It seems to me terrible that men should be asked to undergo the blighting experience of a gaol sentence because of attempts of officialdom to crush any organized protest by these men against insufferable conditions imposed upon them. Public opinion in British Columbia finally demanded and secured their release.
Again, I visited the camps in British Columbia which were provided for those who were described as eastern transients, that is the men who, it was claimed, had residence at points east of the great lakes. There again I found difficulties. It might be interesting to the house to know the conditions which prevailed there. I have no criticism to offer of the officials of the forestry department of British Columbia who were in charge. We visited the camps through the courtesy of Mr. Manning, the chief forester, and Mr. Forse, supervisor of the camps. As far as I could discover, their attitude was completely sympathetic and they were attempting to deal with the problem with some vision. Nevertheless they had turned over to them for the performance of specific tasks men who were in a very bad condition as far as their
health, clothing and general outlook on life were concerned, and I appreciate the fact that the officials had tremendous difficulties.
But in the camps set aside for the eastern transients the men were expected to work a 44-hour week for wages at the rate of thirty cents an hour. These wages were not paid in cash. The net earnings were credited to each man and applied toward the estimated cost of his transportation to eastern Canada. The sum of $5.31 was deducted weekly for board and workmen's compensation. Each man was allowed to draw against his credit amounts for personal necessities to the value of SI.25 weekly and clothing to the value of $16 for the working period, from the camp commissariat. That amount was originally S10, was then raised to $12, and finally to $16. After the clothing allowance was paid for, the man received a net credit of $6.64 for a full working week until the total accumulated credit equalled the return transportation cost, plus the deferred pay of $8 supposed to be for payment upon arrival at point of destination.
At the time I visited the camp it was estimated that a man from the maritime provinces might work eleven or twelve weeks and then be shipped east on his own earnings. At that time these men were not getting a cent in cash although they were working eight hours daily. Each man got goods to the value of $1.25 a week from the commissariat for personal necessities. I found several men suffering from toothache, and in order to get an extraction they found it necessary to trade off various articles they had obtained at the commissariat.. If a man wanted to make himself presentable and get his clothes fixed up by a farmer's wife in the neighbourhood, he had to trade off various things he had acquired from the commissariat. These conditions were not wholesome. To a certain extent these difficulties were ironed out following a personal investigation by the chief forester and negotiations with the Minister of Labour. The whole atmosphere of the camp was one of smouldering rebellion and frustration. The men felt that they were reduced to that low stage of beggary and subjection, with complete isolation from all social amenities, where nothing more worse could happen them.
That is not the end of the story. Since visiting these camps I have met some of these men in eastern Canada; they have called at my office in this building. They left the camps and were given transportation to the east, with two four-dollar cheques to provide for their immediate needs. As far as I could discover, not any of these men could establish domicile at any point in eastern Canada.

speechtext: Let him go to Charlottetown.

speechtext: I know that in a number of hostels men are not admitted without a medical examination, and if there is need for hospital care it is given. I had occasion to make inquiries to-day with respect to an institution in Montreal, and I was told that all who were admitted to that hostel for single unemployed men were first given a medical examination and that if there was any illness they were sent to hospital for proper care.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: As far as my personal knowledge goes, it is only in urgent cases that they will admit men unless they have the necessary residential qualifications in the community. In many of the smaller towns and cities they ship a man out of town quickly. A man has to be desperately ill to get into a hospital. The hostels are overcrowded, and men are sent iback while convalescent and under conditions that make it impossible for them to make an effective recovery. Surely the minister will not minimize that aspect of the situation, because it is serious and has led to loss of life and permanent impairment of the health of a large number of men.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: My hon. friend has referred to the number of accidents that have occurred to transients while riding on freight trains. He gave the figure for 1938 as 120; that is my recollection. Has he inquired as to the number of transients who lost their lives before this present period of depression, back in 1928 and 1929? He will find that there were just as many accidents at that time as there are now, suggesting that they were as a result of the fact of men riding on freight trains illegally, and under conditions affording the minimum of safety. It is not in any way on account of relief conditions or relief administration. I mention that because there is no reason why we should confuse the issue.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I was coming to that, but
this is a special problem that does not arise only out of the depression. If we solved the general unemployment problem to-morrow we should still have the problem of the homeless migrant. I was about to refer to the findings of the Canadian welfare council on this particular point, and I intend to quote from their booklet, because they have stated the problem in lucid language. We are all under a great debt to the members of the
committee who compiled these two studies, "The Problem of the Non-Resident and Migrant," and "Wayfarers Perforce." These pamphlets recently issued by the council discuss the conditions that prevail in the primary industries, agriculture, lumbering, mining anc fishing. I quote:
These occupations, subject anywhere to fluctuating employment conditions, are peculiarly susceptible to heavy seasonal variations in oui climate, which is true also of our other great outlet for comparable labour, construction, in which the average working year is but 26 weeks. Further, the extent of the Canadian territory and the wide distribution of these primary activities over it demanded not only that there by this large reservoir of comparatively young labour, but that it be mobile, ready to shift suddenly from one part of the country to the other. . . .
So, not at all as a depression problem but as a normal feature of our employment structure, Canada has long had a large floating population of men who -were part of the raw material of her development in agriculture, mining, lumbering, fishing and construction.
They also analyse the situation carefully as it has arisen in recent years, showing that owing to the exhaustion of free land, marketing problems, the spread of mechanization in agriculture there has been a back-log in that industry, which has created a condition of incessant trekking across Canada that is becoming more acute and certainly more dangerous in its effects on the lives of the men concerned.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Is there a large percentage
of these young men who really want to get work? I ask only for information. Is that their wish?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Speaking from personal
observation and contact with the men, I say that the great majority of them desire work. My experience has been, when the question has arisen and I have secured the cooperation of large employers of labour-I refer particularly to the manager of a large mine in British Columbia-some of these men were offered work, accepted the work and I followed up their records with the company and found that they gave satisfactory service when so employed. All they were asking was a type of employment which was not a blind alley. Once they got employment that offered some future, some permanency, some hope of advancement, some opportunity to learn something, they grasped it eagerly. The Canadian welfare council goes on to say:
As we all know, labour supply and demand is not confined within provincial boundaries. Many of the largest employers of labour are Canadian corporations, operating on a dominionwide basis, and they may move their employees or "gangs" from province to province and from
2876	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
one part of a province to another. Consequently a man may have a fairly continuous record of work, spread over different provinces with short seasonal breaks, and yet he may be utterly unable to establish residence in any province of Canada. He may have been born and brought up in one of the maritime provinces, but his settlement may have been lost by five years continuous residence outside that province. Yet he may not have worked in any other centre long enough to have acquired a new legal residence.
I think they make a convincing case that our present residential qualifications have severely aggravated the problem. There is no uniformity in residential qualifications across Canada. The council has classified the non-residents or migrants into four main classifications: local residents, provincial residents, interprovincial residents, and migrants or casuals, and have suggested a practical plan, in my opinion, to deal with this matter. I think it important that this plan should be brought to the attention of the house. It is stated succinctly, and I think it is something that should be put into effect without any delay. They say, in the "The Program-in Summary," incorporated in "Wayfarers Perforce" :
Consequently, the control of the problem of dependent non-resident persons would appear to call for:
1. As the liability of the provinces-
The enactment by each province of Canada of comparable residence legislation which will set up uniform practices in each for-
(1)	the acquisition of legal residence at tjie expiration of a specified period of self-supporting residence therein, or, alternatively, at the expiration of a much longer period, for persons dependent upon social aid within that time.
(2)	reciprocal action among the respective municipalities therein, whereby legal residence will not be lost within one municipality until acquired within another, and with reciprocal adjustment of costs of maintenance, when necessary.
(3)	reciprocal action between the province itself, and its respective municipalities to provide for the establishment of legal residence within the province as a whole for persons who may have lost or never had legal residence within any one municipality therein, and the adjustment of maintenance costs accordingly.
(4)	reciprocal action among the different provinces of Canada for the registration, and if need be, maintenance or alternatively, orderly return of persons with established legal residence within one found without such legal residence in another.
Then they go on to deal with the liability of the dominion, with several useful concrete suggestions. It is true that a man may have been bom and brought up in Ontario, may leave the province in a legitimate attempt to secure work in western Canada, move from point to point as the work develops, probably land finally in British Columbia, and on returning to Ontario within perhaps two years
[Mr. MacXeil.l
have completely lost all residential qualification or "rights of domicile" in Ontario. That, I think, largely accounts for the seriously aggravated problem with which we are confronted at the moment.
May I suggest to the minister that the problem is going to be still more acute, certainly in British Columbia, according to the information now reaching me, because the camps there are about to close. In Vancouver the situation is acute. I have here the statement of the superintendent of Abbot house, giving the following information:

Men interviewed	 9,618 15,795 12,518
Free meals issued.. .. 19,614 30,717 31,231 Free beds issued	 5,618 13,937 13,861
And I am informed that' according to the last report the situation is growing rapidly worse.
Here I think something may be done. The federal government should give leadership. They extend grants in aid to the provincial governments for assisting unemployment relief. These grants in aid are made subject to certain conditions or stipulations. The provincial governments, if they accept the grants, are required to carry out these conditions. I see no objection to the federal government also stipulating that the provincial governments shall secure uniformity with regard to residential qualifications among municipalities within the province. I see no reasonable objection to the federal government stipulating that there shall be reciprocal arrangements, not only uniformity of residential qualifications across the dominion but reciprocal arrangements so that transients who are making a legitimate effort to secure work may when in distress apply to the proper authority for aid, and receive such aid without the present difficulties. It seems to me the height of absurdity, it seems even insane, that under the conditions described by the welfare council by which we require men to show some enterprise in seeking work under the circumstances that prevail in Canada, we should immediately penalize them for their enterprise. Yet that is exactly the situation existing in Canada to-day. I recommend to the consideration of the house the final words of the report of the welfare council:
The importance of bringing about greater uniformity in our procedures concerning residence cannot be overstressed nor can we overemphasize either the values attached to properly organized works and training projects as contrasted to direct aid. But the especial significance of this latter statement, as it concerns this problem lies in the fact that, we must constantly avoid the tendency, which is perhaps only natural under our system of local responsibility, to exclude the "outsiders" or

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
non-residents from the special measures of aid or rehabilitation that a community devises for its "own" people.
Some one has said or written that "pioneers built this country." Pioneers had to move about from community to community, from province to province, from coast to coast. And it is difficult to see why Canada, still so largely a pioneer country, needing, as she does, with her seasonal variations and primary industrial occupations, a seasonal mobile labour corps, can fail to see that the ultimate development of our entire country will be retarded if we allow the idea to become prevalent that remaining in one spot for the purpose of being assured of aid is to be preferred over the spirit that impels another person to risk the loss of eligibility for aid by moving off in search of work.

speechtext:
During this debate this house and the Canadian people have been listening for some hint from some speaker showing the possibility of a solution of this problem of unemployment. Unquestionably there must be a solution. As has been reiterated time and again, if this country could not produce the milk and cream, the butter and eggs and cheese, the lumber and brick and every other thing that the people of this country need to give them a high standard of living, then indeed there would be cause for anxiety. But the fact that this country can produce in great abundance and variety and of high quality practically everything which the people of this country need for a high standard of living indicates beyond question that there must be a solution. The people of this country have been looking for some hint of that solution to come out of this debate.
Thus far there have been three outstanding and perhaps typical speeches, I would say: that of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) ; that of the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette), which was probably the typical Liberal reaction, and that of the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman), which was very difficult to classify in any serious way at all. Each of the other speeches, apart from those delivered by the outlaws, so to speak, fell within one of these classes. These three speeches, together with the record of the Conservative administration between 1930 and 1935 and that of the Liberal administration from 1935 until the present time, testify against the old-line parties and constitute a convincing and condemning bit of evidence as to the intellectual bankruptcy, financial decrepitude and incompetence of both these parties. It is easy enough to stand up and advocate an elaborate system of reforestation or an elaborate system of water control or elaborate highway systems; a twelve year old boy with ordinary intelligence anywhere in the Dominion of Canada would suggest
those things and know they ought to be done. Why we should spend a great deal of time in this house discussing such matters is more than I can see.
The speeches of a number of members of the government and their supporters remind me of the title of a play, The Doll's House. As boys we usually found it difficult to play house without finding the play rather tedious and unsubstantial; but our ministers of the crown seem to be carefully schooled nowadays. They have endured this sort of unsubstantial dolls' play for three years with an astonishing amount of complacency, and occasionally they even manage to whip up some enthusiasm about their shallow play, which completely amazes me.
One of the best examples of this unsubstantial make-believe to which we have been treated and which a number of people seem to find rather satisfying is our youth training program. Let me hasten to point out that I value the youth training program, but I think anyone who tries to be at all realistic must acknowledge that it has been a great disappointment. To illustrate what I say let me refer to a booklet which I have in my hand, beautifully prepared, beautifully printed, attractive and romantic, entitled, Training Canada's Young Unemployed. At page 24 I find that in 1937-38 there were 55,457 young people trained in Canada, out of which number there were 3,282 employed. I wish to be perfectly just, so I will point out that at the bottom of this page it is stated that only 14,649 of these young people finished the courses. Even at that, only 22-4 per cent of those who finished the courses found employment.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me, I think the statement is rather that of those taking the courses leading to employment, that percentage were placed. Physical training and rural courses naturally were not designed to lead directly to new employment.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Thank you. I needed only that comment by the minister to finish my contention as to the unsubstantiality of this program. If we set to work to solve our problem of unemployment by giving our young people training in dancing and in forest lore and general conditioning, then I think we are really getting out of touch with realities.

This whole thing reminds me of my boyhood, when I used to attempt to satisfy a six-inch appetite by eating dainty, fluffy inch-square sandwiches supplemented with milk in an inch-deep play dinner cup. Of course the play dinner was better than nothing, but imagine trying to live for years on play dinner banquets! Evidently that is what the government is endeavouring to teach the people of Canada to do.
I am now going to turn for a few moments to the speech of the hon. member for Huron North. I should like to point out that while there have been several who have occasionally taken flings at us, I think hon. members will agree that we have very rarely answered them. We have taken the attitude that the people who had unkind things to say about us just did not know what they were talking about, so why worry about them. Personally I can easily remember the time when I would have said just such foolhardy things as have been said in this house, and that time was only four years ago. But I know that whereas I was blind, now I see; and I know that while they are blind now, soon the day will come when they will see. Otherwise they probably will be mercifully removed from the scene of action so that more intelligent people may take their places. That may sound strong, but we could say stronger things than that if we took the notion. But I am going to say a word or two about the speech of the hon. member for Huron North. He has been here long enough to know better.

speechtext: He will never learn.

speechtext:
We will tell him about it, anyway. The hon. member, without making any contribution himself, saw fit to undertake to ridicule the social credit proposals. I am going to read a passage from his speech, appearing at page 2770 of Hansard:
What have we from the different parties or groups? We have our friends the social crediters. What is their program? Always it is the same thing-more money, scrip! They are the scrip tease artists of Canadian politics. But all this scrip teasing never eventuates in anything. We go on trying the same thing, but there is always the same idea in the background: if only we had money.
May I break in there to point out that this last is the statement of every hon. member of this house; and of all hon. members the one who most frequently uses it is the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). Yet because we

social crediters -use it also, it is supposed to be a reflection upon our intelligence. How far a man who prides himself on possessing a measure of intelligence will let himself get off the track of reason and common sense! Now I go further:
Goods do not matter, give the people money. Money enables a man to purchase goods, and when you give him money you give him goods. When you give him goods you are giving him something for which you or someone else must work. You cannot settle the problem with currency issued on the unshot buffaloes of Canada or the uncaught fish of Alberta.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: What a brain!

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
An hon. member says, "what a brain!" I say, what a shameful abuse of an otherwise good brain! I will comment in a few minutes on some of the remarks. I say, at the outset, that it would be exceedingly difficult for a man to put into that amount of space more absolutely foolhardy remarks than that man succeeded in putting into that one little passage- more distortions of the facts, more misunderstandings, more misinterpretations, more misconceptions, more absolute untruths. The hon. member is inaccurate in his learning, his understanding and his reasoning, as shown in this passage. As an inaccuracy, for example, may I point out that he says, "more money, scrip." May I point out to the hon. member [DOT]-and I see he is not in his seat; I had hoped he would be, because I want to talk to him 

that not once in this house has the word "scrip" been used by any member of this group.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Shame.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
It is a shame for a man to go to work and make a statement like that, in the face of that condition. He was put-well, I will not say that. We will let people draw their own conclusions as to why he put that in there. In spite of what the hon. member has said, we have never said anything about scrip in this house or outside it. The first thing we pointed out was that this government ought to have purchasing power. We have advocated state money, currency and credit, just as the Prime Minister of Canada advocated currency and credit. Yet when we advocate the same thing we are scrip teasers. Think of that, for intelligent reasoning!
I have referred to the $26,000,000 printed by the government between 1915 and 1917, and used by the government for governmental purposes. According to the hon. member for Huron North I presume that was scrip. I have referred to the Bradburys experiment in England, as a result of which
APRIL 17, 1939	2S79
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
Great Britain was able to fight the war. I presume that was scrip! I wonder if the hon. member would call either one of those scrip. If so, we do not mind being called scrip teasers. But the difficulty is that many misinformed people throughout the country who read Hansard are deliberately-no, I will not say that-but the hon. member allows them to be able to form misconceptions of the contentions of a group of people whom that hon. member knows to be sincere in their contentions, at a time when no one in the dominion parliament knows what to do in order to solve the problem. And the discussion of the last three days abundantly proves it.
What ails the mentality of men like the hon. member for Huron North? He makes the remark about our being scrip teasers. That is a great compliment to this group. We were sent here to advocate monetary reform, because after a more careful study than I ever heard of people making, in the history of the world, the people in our province came to the conclusion that the only solution of world problems lay in monetary reform. They sent us here to advocate such monetary reform and we have done it. We have done it consistently, in season and out of season, in the face of all sorts of attitudes. We take it as a compliment that we are called scrip teasers.
May I point out to the hon. member for Huron North, and to a good many other hon. members, for whom he was speaking- if they are here-that if the Liberals had been better teasers for some of the things they were sent here to advocate and to get, this country would be farther on the way to recovery. If they had brought to the attention of their Prime Minister the fact that he undertook to remove poverty from the midst of plenty; if they had insisted upon it- teased upon it-and if they had called upon him to make good his promises about monetary reform, or if they had insisted that some time before the next election he should commence that famous battle with the money powers, and had teased a little bit about it, we would probably have had him engaged in battling against the money powers instead of apparently letting somebody else do all the fighting while he remains impassive and inactive, and allows the money powers to go calmly on their way.
The hon. member for Huron North uses the expression, "goods do not matter, give the people money." I point out to every hon. member in the house, and to this particular one, if he cares to read it in Hansard, that the very first thing this group did when it
came to the House of Commons was to point out that there was an abundance, that there was plenty. Canada had solved the problem of production. And yet this hon. member has the effrontery to imply that we disregard goods. When we came to this house, the air and the press were full of remarks about over-production. Over-production means only one thing, and that is a surplus of goods. How in the world when there is a recognized surplus of goods everywhere could you by issuing money be disregarding goods?

My hon. friend cannot understand anything but politics. He is now dealing with a group which is not concerned with politics, but which is concerned with the welfare of the children of its members and of his children.
If we can go forward now, perhaps a word should be said at this point on this particular matter. The question has been raised, and I should like to direct the attention of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) to the fact that he is now giving relief to people who do not work. Why is it that when we propose to give a dividend of $25 to everybody, immediately the objection is raised that we are giving a regular income to people who do not work? It is just a matter of degree. The governments are now providing an income to relief recipients in such a niggardly fashion that we are destroying the body economic and the body social of this country. Beyond any shadow of a doubt we are destroying the morale of the people. We are destroying their ability to marry, to have children and to support their families. We are destroying the very body and soul of this Dominion of Canada simply because of the meagre stipend we are giving. This is totally inadequate end yet these men cannot supplement it by getting a job. The minute they do get a job their relief is cut off, as has been indicated by many good speeches to-day. If anything in the world is designed to discourage initiative, to discourage a willingness to work, it is the system which the minister is applying to-day in this dominion. To raise this objection against our proposals is not to indicate that clarity of thought which the minister ordinarily possesses.
I am now going on with the question of how the social crediters define money in relation to goods. When I was interrupted I was

endeavouring to point out that we have contended consistently that this is an age of plenty. As evidence of our contention may I point out that one of the greatest writers on the social credit theory is Mr. C. Marshall Hattersley. This gentleman has published a book entitled, This Age of Plenty, which indicates beyond any shadow of a doubt that he takes for granted, first, that there is plenty, and then, the possibility of the creation of money in relation to goods. I am glad to see the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) in the house. If the hon. member had paid as close attention to the social credit proposal as his speech seemed to indicate he thought he had paid, he would have known that long ago. A speech which he delivered on March 14, 1938, indicates quite clearly that he had in mind that there was an abundance of goods. I regret that I have not the page of Hansard, but these are his words:
While it might in normal times, or would in normal times, be employed in the production of capital goods-
He is. as I recall it, speaking of the money which is on hand.

it does not now go back into the production of capital goods because money is invested in capital goods for the production of consumer goods, and if there is no demand for consumer goods then money will not flow in capital production.
The goods are there, here and everywhere; they are in our stores; they are on our shelves, and yet there is no effective demand for those goods. The social credit proposal is to create that effective demand for those goods. Yet the hon. member, along with the whole brotherhood of hectic-minded devotees of his type are ready to claim that the social creditors disregard goods!

speechtext:
I beg the pardon of the hon. member for Huron North for having given him the thought that I would think of that kind of word. The hon. member for Huron North speaks of giving goods or something which someone else has worked to produce. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning', made a good deal of that the other day. 1 have not the page of Hansard upon which he is reported; but if my memory serves me aright he stated that if you created a dollar biL and gave it to somebody, you gave to that person the power to force someone else tc redeem that dollar bill with goods that someone else had worked for. I suppose that is the idea which is in the mind of the hon member for Huron North. I can forgive him more easily for that misunderstanding than 1 can for the other, but I am going to forgive him completely. I shall leave it entirely to misapprehension or the inability to apprehend I am going to point out to the hon. membei for Huron North and to every other person in this country who has been deceived in the same way, that we already have in this country an abundance of means of storing wealth which represent work which someone else has done.
I shall refer to a few classes of this kind. In the first place we have goods. We have an abundance of wheat, fish, shoes, brick, lumber and furniture, just to mention a few. Work has already been done in the production of these goods. But these goods are lying' idle and falling into decay, and the fact that these goods which have been produced by the hard work of men are being wasted seems not to cause my hon. friend even the slightest amount of distress. Why can he not see that having worked to produce lumber, for example, a man would be far happier to see that lumber given to someone to make a house than he would to see it lying in decay in the lumber yard. It is this lying in decay which appears not to disturb the members of the present government. It is that fact which seems entirely to escape their attention.
Let me turn to another kind of wealth, a type of wealth which has needed an abundance of work to produce. All over this country we have factories, railroads, farm equipment, mining machinery, fishing equipment and lumbering equipment. According to the
2882	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
March, 1939, monthly letter of the Bank of Commerce, industry in Canada to-day is only 69 per cent occupied. In other words, 31 per cent of the potential capacity of the industry of Canada is lying idle. This represents that upon which work has been expended to produce. Is the hon. member for Huron North at all concerned that this work should be wasted, that it should lie idle? He is, but he does not realize how much he is neglecting it; for if an industry is allowed to lie idle, the work which produced that industry is going to waste. There is no other way in which an intelligent man can interpret the matter.
Not only is industry lying idle and going to waste, but we have capital in this country. The hon. member for Huron North has said several times on the floor of this house, even in the speech from which I quoted, that much of our capital to-day is unable to find profitable investment. It is going into government securities. That is cause for alarm to the hon. member and it is cause for alarm to every informed individual in this country. But merely to point out the difficulty is not to find the solution. The solution lies in so adjusting the economy of this country that industry will be able to find sufficient markets to encourage the putting into it of the money which is lying idle. It is all a question of these markets and how to obtain them. If we neglect to put purchasing power into the hands of the people to provide those markets we are thereby forcing the capital of the country, which has cost the work of millions of men through scores of years, to lie idle and consequently to waste.
Money or capital represents work that someone else has done. Much money now is idle, invested in mortgages at a loss, invested in homes and property at a loss, invested in government securities at a low rate of interest, when it should be deriving a larger rate of interest through investment in profitable industries; lying idle, again at a loss. But the loss of the result of the work which went into the production of that capital is not, apparently, distressing the members of this government at all. They do not realize that they have the responsibility of protecting the things which cost work. They are causing to be lost, that which cost work. But the minute we propose the creation of one dollar bill in Canada to put in the hands of a widow, for example, so that she can buy a dollar's worth of coal, so that the producer can sell the coal for money he can spend, and so that the miner can produce another ton of coal, we are told that we are "giving away" something which somebody else worked 
for. Well, any mind which cannot see the absolute absurdity of such reasoning as our opponents follow needs to be retrained.
There is another product of work in this country which is being neglected. What is there in Canada which requires more work to produce than a man? Into the production of what being has gone more work of heart and soul and body than the production of a man? Somebody's mother produced every single one of those transients and every one of those unemployed. Somebody's father strove and toiled to raise each of those boys. Are we caring about the waste of that work? Not one bit.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: They are afraid to give a dollar.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Rather than protect the work that these loving souls put into raising that man-I think I will start it in another way; I was going to say something a little too harsh. We will not create one dollar of new money. We will not depart from the sacred rules of high finance in order to protect that precious heritage, that precious possession-a human being. One rule of the laws of high finance handed down to us from five generations ago is of more value in this government's sight than are these men.
It cost work to produce the intellect of a man. Think of the teachers who have toiled to cultivate the intellect of a man; think of what the mother, the father and the neighbours have done for him. Do the powers that be care about all that work? Not at all. It can go to waste.
Think of the work the man himself has been put to in training himself through five or seven years, perhaps even a longer period of hard work, to condition and equip himself to fill a niche in the economic life of the country. Are we caring about the work which went intq that man's training? Not at all. It can go to waste. Before the hon. member for Huron North vented his scorn upon the people who have or at least think they have the way out, why could he not think his way through, just a little?

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I have.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: The hon. member needs to do a good deal more thinking. I can remember when I was at his stage, a good many years ago. He says that you cannot settle the problem with currency issued on the unshot buffaloes of Canada, on the uncaught fish of Alberta.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
A lot of fish are caught in Alberta 1

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: There are more fish caught in the Liberal party.

maintopic: UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
To comment upon that for just a minute or two, did not the banks, in the days when they used to advance a line of credit to the farmers, advance money-credit against unproduced grain which the farmer was going to raise? Of course they did. Then why not upon uncaught fish or unshot cattle? If the hon. member wanted to be really accurate he would have said " cattle " instead of " buffaloes ''-that is, if he had not been trying so hard to be funny.
When banks loaned freely to producers over Canada, men everywhere got jobs and got money, and they bought goods which the producers could sell. But the hon. member contends that you cannot " settle " your problem. True, Mr. Speaker, you cannot settle your problem with any device, but you can help to settle it. When a man is stricken with peritonitis and near to death you cannot solve his problem with a knife, but you can help to solve it if you are skilful enough to use the knife aright. I maintain that the peritonitis from which this country is suffering cannot be solved except by the use of a device which has not yet been tried. You cannot settle without currency, used upon goods already waiting effective demand to buy them, and upon uncaught fish and unmined coal and unsawn lumber and ungenerated electricity and unfabricated woollens, rayons, automobiles, paper, et cetera. I will lay that down as a principle and it will never be challenged successfully. You cannot solve your problems until you do have currency and credit issued upon such items of real wealth-goods.
What is the fundamental cause of unemployment? I am not going to discuss this to any great extent to-night, because others have not been discussing it and we have been called to order when we attempted to discuss it. You can talk all you like about our troubles, but you must not talk about the solution. However, there are one or two things I am going to say in the few minutes which are left to me. What is the fundamental cause of unemployment? It is lack of money. There are many people who say that is not so. I am not now going to take the trouble to read something which I shall read at a later time. This is a set of figures shown on page 53 of Senator Owen's National Economy and the Banking System. It shows conclusively that where the amount of money in circulation in a country falls, unemployment grows; where the amount of money in circulation increases, unemployment falls off. Hon.
members can read it. I shall put it on Hansard later on, when I have more time. It shows that the cause of unemployment is lack of money, the hon. member for Huron North to the contrary notwithstanding.
What is the remedy? The remedy is adequate banking management. I am going to read a passage by William A. Shaw, no social erediter or monetary reformer or unorthodox thinker, but one of the most orthodox of men. This man is secretary to the editor of the calendar of treasury records of his majesty's government. I am about to read from a book called, Principles of Currency, Credit and Exchange, By William A. Shaw and Alfred Wigglesworth. This book is in the library. I am reading from page 52:
In enunciating for the banks the simple principle which must guide them in this task of controlling an upward or prosperity phase, it is not difficult to lay down a rough-and-ready datum line from which to start. That line is simply such a level of prosperity as will keep the whole of our economic system functioning healthily, and will provide suitable sustenance to every man, woman and child in the land, and suitable employment to every employable person-

say something on this occasion. In the course of my remarks on Thursday last I made the following statement:
. . . thousands have died as a result of exposure, illness, actual starvation or lack of care.
I chose that language carefully, and I expressed it, I felt, with equal care. If it is examined in its entirety it will be found that it does not say that thousands have died as a result of starvation, which is the only interpretation put upon my words by some. I used the phrase, "exposure, illness, actual starvation or lack of care." Surely these words are about as broad in their meaning as any words could be. "Lack of care" itself is a phrase which embraces much. For example, as a result of lack of care it is fully possible that one person would move from one place to another. Accordingly, in using that phrase as I did I meant to include the accidents that have resulted on the various railways, on highways and in similar ways. In fact, in answer to a question from the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean), I used the word "accident."

This afternoon I commenced my remarks with a reference to an article which appeared in the issue of March 15, 1939 of Maclean's magazine, by the Hon. G. M. Thousands of wasted lives and millions of wasted dollars could be saved by an adequate health policy, says this authority.

The public dependents alone number 1,500,000 and there are at least as many others who fall in the class of medically indigent.

Our day to day experience with many hundreds of families shows conclusively that there are many people in the city of Toronto who are not getting enough to eat.

I do not suggest that all of these would necessarily have survived if they had received such care, but surely it is a fair inference that some of them at least would not have died had they been financially able to obtain medical service.
Finally, may I refer to another publication of the bureau of statistics, entitled, Statistics of the Steam Railways of Canada, 1937. On page 42 we note the statement that for the years 1932 to 1937 inclusive, 918 persons were killed while trespassing on the property of the Canadian railways, and 1,496 were injured. It may be assumed that the majority of those killed and injured were unquestionably indigent transients.
There are no figures available in the bureau of statistics, I am informed, as to the number of indigent transient pedestrians who have been killed on the highways. Hon. members all know personally of such cases.
In conclusion, in the light of such statistical evidence as exists in support of the statement I have made, I ask the minister to withdraw his adjective, "irresponsible" or in the alternative to give a clear indication to the committee of the extent to which he considers my statement in error. I do not believe he is prepared to go to the length of maintaining that no one has died as a result of lack of care, or to the extent of saying that those who have done so are insignificant in number. He realizes, as I do, that to obtain full and complete statistical evidence of those who have died as a result of malnutrition or undernutrition or whatever the case may be, or those who have died as a result of lack of care, is difficult. So, clearly from those figures one cannot possibly draw a conclusion which reflects upon the administration of relief or policies with respect to unemployment. There were more of these unfortunate deaths among transients in the years preceding the administration of relief than have occurred in these recent years.
So far as malnutrition is concerned, I wish to refer to a statement given by the deputy minister of pensions and national health in the preface to the National Health Review, and to a study of nutrition in Canada which was made by a special committee for the British Commonwealth Scientific Conference. These are the words of the deputy minister in respect of nutrition:
The principal findings of the subcommittee as given in this brief report show that in respect to Canada:
(1)	There is an abundance of food of different varieties sufficient to give balanced diets containing all essentials.
(2)	These can be provided under the existing government rates of assistance to families of the unemployed.
(3)	Economical menus or diets, adequate for the maintenance of health, have been suggested for the use of people of all ages.
(4)	There is no evidence of increased incidence of nutritional ailments among the children since 1929; in fact, there wipuld appear to be a reduction, owing to organized welfare work everywhere, With fewer missed cases. There is a halt in the decline of the tuberculosis death rate, but its importance is not yet admitted to be due to dietary causes.
I would also refer to a special study made by the director of social services in McGill university, Professor L. C. Marsh, in which he states that there has been less actual want, and in recent years more medical care during the depression than before. I think most hon. members will acknowledge that through the relief administration, and the medical attention attached to that, we have had developed in these recent years for the total population a far greater degree of medical attention than we have ever enjoyed before.
There may be hon. members who will still say that this attention is not adequate. But certainly in what I have submitted to the committee at this time there is not the slightest evidence to substantiate the suggestion of the hon. member for Greenwood that through inadequate relief administration there has been a marked increase in deaths, as a result of malnutrition. As a matter of fact malnutrition does not arise entirely from lack of food. There may be malnutrition, with great quantities of food available. It arises rather from a lack of balanced diet.
To sum up, I submit my hon. friend has failed entirely to produce any more evidence in support of his original statement than he did when that statement was made and challenged in the house. And I suggest it would have been far better had he withdrawn that statement then, particularly in view of the natural deductions which would be based upon it with respect to relief administration in this country. He has not seen fit to do so; that is a matter entirely for his conscience. But I submit to the committee that the statement was unfortunate and without foundation, and that it ought to have been withdrawn when it was made originally.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise only
to address one or two remarks to the minister in virtue of the fact that he requested me to refrain from interrupting him, which I was happy to do. The minister has left the impression with the committee that there has been an inordinately small number of those in this dominion who have died from starvation or malnutrition. The figures he gave are figures which I myself knew existed at the bureau, and I have seen them.
On the other hand he must know that malnutrition is an indirect rather than a direct cause of death, and that as a result of malnutrition such diseases as tuberculosis, pneumonia, stomach ulcers and other such ailments are brought about. The further result is that upon the death certificates of those who have been undernourished there appear such well known diseases as those I have mentioned. I am sure the minister will agree with me in that statement.
Second, the minister points out the fact that transients-if we may call them such- who before 1929 were killed on the railroads, and transients who have been killed on the railroads since 1929 are about equal in number. Mr. Chairman, surely what was wrong yesterday and prevails to-day is not made right by the fact that it prevails to-day. I was endeavouring to the best of my ability to bring to the attention of the minister the

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
plight of those who are within the country to-day and who are faced with the problems of relief-for they are problems-the problems of unemployment, low wages, and part-time, not only among our youth but among our people of all ages. And I have noticed tonight that in the minister's reply to the statement I had made he seemed to be more anxious to justify the present relief administration than to recognize the condition which exists in this country from coast to coast.
I am not concerned about what conditions were five years ago or six years ago or eight years ago nearly so much as I am with conditions which exist to-day, and with what - is going to be done about those conditions which exist to-day. That is the point upon which I stand, and that is what I was endeavouring to bring to the minister's attention in the remarks I made the other day. The minister is not going to stand in his place in this house and say he is satisfied with conditions of relief in this country, and that they cannot be made better? I have placed upon Hansard to-night the figures which show the conditions in my own city of Toronto, where those who are in contact with that situation from day to day, and are in a position to know, people such as medical health officers make statements showing there are conditions prevailing which should not be permitted to exist in any civilized country.
My whole endeavour has been to draw to the attention of the minister and to present to the committee the deplorable conditions prevailing in Canada, conditions which demand the full consideration of this parliament. We are at war within our own country, social war. We have the ways and means of handling the situation in time of war, and we do it without hesitation. I say the situation within our dominion to-day among those who are unemployed and who are underprivileged, from the youngest infant to the oldest man or woman, demands the immediate and most serious attention of the government; and it is in their name I have made this plea in this chamber.

municipalities. On the other hand it is equally important that we remember that in all provinces and all municipalities there are people engaged in the administration of relief who are doing their work well, and whose work ought not to be distorted and misrepresented in this place and to the country at large. I suggest it was originally a very serious reflection which my hon. friend made not only upon those in charge of relief administration throughout this country, but also upon private, voluntary welfare organizations throughout the dominion, and, indeed, upon what one might term the common humanity of us all. His statement was absolutely wide of the facts, and if he declines entirely to withdraw it, then that is a matter for him to decide.

Then I shall speak on the motion as amended. In the absence of the text of the amendment, I shall endeavour to follow the discussion of the minister which, as I remember it, had very little to do with the amendment. As I remember it, the amendment had to do with youth training, and the minister was discussing mortality here, there and yon in all its phases, including mortality among transients. My first observation is that in 1934 the death rate was 9-4 per thousand; in 1935 it was 9-7, and in 1937, it was 10-2. So far there is no twelve month indication for the nine month period .which the minister quoted. We have seen a general rise in the mortality rate.
I should like to make a few remarks based upon actual experience covering the last decade in connection with the responsibility of providing some 537,640 patient days in connection with a hospital over which it has been my privilege to act as president and chairman of the board. In connection with that organization I was fortunate in having associated with me for some years the hon.
2890	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey). Each month the hon. member received a detailed report consisting of some ten foolscap pages, which outlined all the activities of that organization. As I say, this organization has provided over one-half million patient days of service to all classes of hospital patients, ranging from those well able to pay their way to those indigents who are unable to pay anything toward their care. The hon. member knows whereof he speaks. The minister has said that there was not the slightest evidence to back up the statement which the hon. member made, but from my own knowledge I know there is evidence.
The minister has said that the hon. member should let his conscience be his guide, but I say to the minister that he should calmly think over this situation and let his conscience be his guide. The minister said that the facts had been distorted, and he used some other expression which I cannot remember. Perhaps it would not be a bad idea if now and again some emphasis were given in this chamber to certain facts, even to the extent of going beyond the ordinary, in order to wake up and get some action from the administration in connection with one of the most vital and difficult problems which Canada has to face to-day.
Let me give a few facts. I have just received a letter from the auditors of the Toronto East hospital reciting some facts with regard to the difficulties which they have been encountering over the last three-year period. I should like to mention these difficulties as an illustration of the difficulties which all organizations giving service of this kind have had to meet. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) has been generous in receiving deputations and requests from organizations of this kind. He has given them every consideration, and I believe that in his calm moments he realizes the difficulties faced by organizations which have to look after the class of people to which the hon. member for Greenwood made reference and that class of people requiring hospitalization, to which the minister made reference when he was quoting his statistics.
These institutions find it more and more difficult to balance their budgets because there come to them for service more and more of the indigent class, more and more of those who are on relief, who are able to pay only the minimum for the service they receive. In the final result, those charged with the administration of these institutions find themselves up against a problem which seems almost insurmountable. That problem, as one year succeeds another, becomes more and

more difficult. As time goes on, a greater number of the classes of people of which we have been talking, including transients, those on relief and those unemployed, find themselves physically unable to stand up with the assistance they are getting from the government. If these same individuals were employed their state of mind would be more serene, they would be happier and their health would be better. Then, when they happened to come to these institutions, they would be patients in connection with whom there might be some hope of success. According to the evidence which the minister was kind enough to place on record, our mortality rate is steadily rising. So much for that side of the picture.
I come now to the financial side. It is admitted at once that those who are unable to pay are generally those on relief or transients who have been brought in as a result of accident. Those who know the geography of Toronto and vicinity will appreciate the fact that the Toronto East general hospital is the nearest hospital to the Danforth yard. This is the yard where trains are broken up, and transients from the jungle just outside the Danforth station hop on and off the trains at this point. When accidents occur, they are brought to the Toronto East general hospital. Each Sunday afternoon for the past ten years it has been my pleasure to visit many of these patients. I know from actual observation that the available statistics do not reflect the actual number of those who are killed because of accident, or those who are injured and subsequently pass out. They do not indicate the number of those to whom service is given in these different institutions, service made necessary because of malnutrition. Many of these patients are not able to stand the effect of an operation.
Progress reported.
